en.hype: One of the hardest tables to get in Tokyo.
en.reality: 4.5 on Google from 220 reviews, and a Tabelog Bronze medal every year since 2019. Bookings open about a month ahead and dinner slots go within hours.
en.tip: Bookings open about a month ahead and cost JPY 2,000 per person. Get ready for opening day.
en.baby_notes: Small counter with ten seats, no private rooms. Adults only.
en.serves: Edo-style chef's counter meal, old Tokyo cooking. A seasonal course of small dishes handed straight to your plate by the chef.
en.todo: Reservations only, don't just turn up. About 50,000 yen per person in the evening, and on some days there is also a 44,000 yen breakfast. With a baby, ask them first whether it works.
en.special: An intimate counter and traditional Edo cooking, with every dish coming straight from the chef.
en.kosher_note: Fixed course with a lot of seafood. You can ask when booking for no pork or seafood, but they may not agree.
en.plan_line: Booking essential, closed Sundays and Mondays
en.baby_block: Small counter, adults only

en.hype: Black eggs boiled in volcanic springs are Hakone's viral snack, and the sulphur valley photographs well.
en.reality: The valley is worth the stop and the eggs are fine, but it's one more small expense. The ropeway (about ¥1,370 one way) can close in bad weather.
en.tip: Go on a clear day for the view of Fuji, and dress warm in December, it's cold and windy up there.
en.todo: Take the ropeway over the mountains to the sulphur valley, then walk a short trail past steam vents and a strong sulphur smell. Buy black eggs and eat them on the spot. On a clear day you can see Fuji from here.
en.special: An active volcanic area with steam coming out of the ground, and eggs whose shells turn black from the minerals.
en.plan_line: Check in the morning that the ropeway is running
en.baby_block: Sulphur fumes, not recommended with a baby

en.hype: A basement cocktail bar with over 10 fruit cocktails, cigars and modern technique.
en.reality: 4.5 on Google from about 196 reviews, and people call it one of the best cocktail bars they've been to. Also on the 2022 Tabelog 100.
en.tip: The bar is in a basement opposite the Tokyo Metropolitan Theatre, and the one to order is a fruit cocktail.
en.baby_notes: Not suitable for babies: a basement cigar bar, an adults' night out.
en.serves: Fresh fruit cocktails that change with the season, not too sweet, and you really taste the fruit. There are also classics and cigars.
en.todo: There's no clear info on booking or entry, so call or check their Instagram first. It's an evening bar, and the basement may be smoky from cigars. With a baby it's not the place, better that one couple goes without the baby.
en.special: Entered Asia's 50 Best Bars in 2025 at number 49, and moved up to 39 in the 2026 ranking.
en.kosher_note: A cocktail bar, drinking there is no problem.
en.plan_line: Better to book a seat ahead
en.baby_block: Basement bar, no stroller space, not suitable for a baby

en.hype: A popular family aquarium inside the Skytree complex.
en.reality: Small and made for kids, so you get through it fast. Open 10:00–20:00 on weekdays and 9:00–21:00 on weekends and holidays.
en.tip: No parking on site, but you can use the Tokyo Skytree Town car park (¥450 per 30 minutes). Last entry is one hour before closing.
en.baby_notes: The Skytree complex has baby rooms and strollers to rent for a coin.
en.price: Free under age 3. Check the adult price on their website.
en.todo: A small indoor aquarium inside Tokyo Solamachi. Do a short loop past fish, jellyfish and the garden eels, and in the middle there's a big pool with penguins and seals you can see up close. It's a 5-minute walk from Oshiage station.
en.special: The open penguin pool is what you'll remember, and everything is small and easy with toddlers.
en.plan_line: On weekends come in the morning before the crowds

en.hype: The wooden terrace on the mountainside is one of the best-known Kyoto photos online.
en.reality: Crowded, but worth it for the view. The street leading up to the temple is very busy during the day.
en.tip: You can also go in the evening if there's a special light-up that season. In December it gets dark early.
en.todo: Climb the steep lanes of Higashiyama, past souvenir and sweet shops, up to the entrance. Inside you pass the red pagoda and reach the big terrace with a view of the city. From there go down to the Otowa waterfall and drink the spring water.
en.special: The huge terrace is built of wood without nails, on tall beams on the mountainside.
en.plan_line: Arrive at 06:00 when it opens, before the crowds
en.baby_block: Steep climb and stairs, hard with a stroller. Take a carrier

en.hype: Grill wagyu and vegetables yourselves on a table grill, great food at an almost unreal price.
en.reality: A casual, crowded place, not fancy.
en.tip: Order the wagyu sets and come early because the place fills up.
en.baby_notes: Table grill and smoke, crowded and no room for a stroller.
en.serves: Yakiniku is meat you grill yourselves on a grill in the middle of the table. Here they serve good wagyu with vegetables on the side.
en.kosher_note: Beef and vegetables. Check the sauces and avoid pork dishes.
en.plan_line: Hours unconfirmed, check Google Maps first
en.baby_block: Smoky grill and no stroller space

en.hype: Old Tokyo lanes, cats and temples, with a feeling that time stopped.
en.reality: A quiet, slow-paced neighbourhood, but it can get busy on weekends.
en.tip: Walk Yanaka Ginza and the cemetery paths, and eat at a local bakery rather than the most photographed shops.
en.todo: Walk around an old Tokyo neighbourhood that wasn't destroyed in the war. Start at the shopping street Yanaka Ginza with its shops and snacks, then go on to the lanes, small temples and Yanaka Cemetery. On the way there are cafes, bakeries and little cat statues.
en.special: Low houses and narrow lanes with no skyscrapers, and the cats are the symbol of the neighbourhood.
en.plan_line: Arrive before 11:30, ahead of the weekend crowds
en.baby_block: Stairs only from Nippori, better from Sendagi station

en.hype: An old dango shop since 1945. There are several kinds, and the winner is the mitarashi dango.
en.reality: A small, simple shop, and the dango is best fresh.
en.tip: Order the mitarashi dango, sticky rice balls in sweet soy sauce, and eat them right away.
en.baby_notes: You can buy takeaway, so the stroller isn't a problem.
en.serves: A Japanese sweets shop selling dango, sticky rice balls on a skewer with sweet sauces.
en.kosher_note: Sweet rice snack, no pork or seafood.
en.plan_line: Open every day, closed only 1–2 January

en.hype: Mocha shaved ice that photographs well, and mochi with azuki.
en.reality: The ice is shaved fine and not too sweet, and the mocha is the one to order. The place is easy to miss and the queue can get long.
en.tip: Open 11:00–18:00. Come at opening or on a weekday to avoid the queue.
en.serves: Mocha kakigori: soft, finely shaved ice with coffee syrup, cream and sweet azuki beans. There's also red mochi with anko, a sweet azuki bean paste.
en.todo: There are only about 4 small tables and a sign in Japanese only. The ice is very cold, so in December it's worth sitting with something hot.
en.special: A small, old-fashioned shop near Sannenzaka that feels like a secret.
en.kosher_note: Ice and azuki desserts, all sweet with no pork or seafood.
en.plan_line: Cash only, closed Tuesdays

en.hype: The famous Glico neon sign over the Dotonbori canal, the most photographed spot in Osaka.
en.reality: A quick stop for a photo, but very crowded. The food around it is the real draw.
en.tip: After the photo, walk away from the crowd and eat nearby.
en.plan_line: Lit in the evening only, shoot from the walkway by Ebisu Bridge

en.hype: A veteran institution since 1939. You choose between a fatty and a lean cut, and cooking takes about 20 minutes.
en.reality: There's usually a queue, and the menu is pork tonkatsu only.
en.tip: Choose between fatty rosu and lean hire.
en.baby_notes: Seating at a very long bar, no room for a stroller.
en.serves: Tonkatsu is a breaded pork cutlet, deep fried and served with shredded cabbage, rice and soup. You choose a fatty or a lean cut.
en.kosher_note: The whole menu is pork, better to skip this place.
en.plan_line: Cash only, closed Tuesday, arrive 16:00 to beat the queue
en.baby_block: Bar seating and a standing queue, no stroller space

en.hype: Considered one of the best ramen shops in Japan.
en.reality: The queue is very long, and the place is far from the centre.
en.tip: Order the thick ramen with fish broth.
en.baby_notes: Far from the centre, long queue outside and a small place, not suitable for a stroller.
en.serves: Ramen is a Japanese noodle soup. Here it's a thick chicken broth with a rich fish broth added, with thick noodles.
en.kosher_note: The broth is chicken and dried fish, but it comes with pork chashu, so ask for none.
en.plan_line: Arrive before 11:00, closed 15:00–18:00
en.baby_block: Small place and a queue outside, not suitable for a stroller

en.hype: A tall bamboo path that's in every Kyoto Instagram feed.
en.reality: The main complaint is the crowds at peak hours, so go when it's quiet.
en.tip: In the middle of the day skip the path and walk to nearby Gio-ji instead.
en.plan_line: Come 6:00–8:00, from 10:00 it's a human traffic jam

en.hype: A quiet pond garden from the Edo period, for people tired of the crowds.
en.reality: A calm oasis with carp and turtles, a short walk from the station. Less than half the garden is wheelchair accessible.
en.tip: Combine it with the cafes and galleries of Kiyosumi-Shirakawa in the same walk.
en.todo: A historic Japanese garden in the Koto area. Walk around a big pond on paths and stepping stones, see carp and turtles, and sit in the tea house on the water's edge. Then carry on to a cafe or the galleries in the neighbourhood.
en.special: A garden built around a pond, with big stones brought from different parts of Japan, and without the tourist crowds.
en.plan_line: Last entry 16:30, closed 29 Dec to 1 Jan
en.baby_block: Gravel path and stepping stones, hard with a stroller

en.hype: An old place run by an elderly woman. You sit around a square bar and eat home cooking with Japanese alcohol.
en.tip: Order the meat stew, it's the best thing there.
en.baby_notes: A small square bar with no room for a stroller. The crowd is mostly older.
en.serves: Japanese home cooking at a small bar, small dishes alongside sake. The recommended dish is a meat stew.
en.kosher_note: Ask whether the meat stew has pork, and don't take the fish dishes.
en.plan_line: Come in the morning before the queue, closed Sundays and Wednesdays
en.baby_block: Small bar, no stroller space

en.hype: A shop with all kinds of things, and everything is 100 yen, about 2.5 shekels.
en.tip: Go up to the fourth floor and pick small gifts.
en.baby_notes: There's a lift, but the aisles between the shelves are narrow.
en.todo: A 100 yen shop with homeware, clothes, toys, stationery and more, on the fourth floor.
en.special: One fixed price for every product.
en.plan_line: Opens 11:00, closes 20:30 on Sundays

en.hype: High-level sushi at a relatively low price, inside an office building. Order omakase.
en.reality: The place is inside an office building and you need to book, so don't just turn up.
en.tip: Order omakase (the chef decides what to serve) and tell the chef ahead what you don't eat.
en.baby_notes: Seating at a sushi counter with no room for a stroller, and a quiet that doesn't suit a baby.
en.serves: Omakase-style sushi: the chef decides and serves piece after piece straight from the counter, with fresh fish.
en.kosher_note: You can eat tuna, salmon, sea bream and white fish, and skip shrimp, squid, octopus, sea urchin, shellfish and eel.
en.plan_line: Busy in the evening, better to book ahead
en.baby_block: Quiet sushi counter, no stroller space

en.hype: A hard-to-book restaurant with high Tabelog ratings, for serious diners.
en.reality: Tabelog 4.52, with Silver every year from 2019 to 2026 and Gold in 2020. One old review finds the food bland for the price.
en.tip: Booking is a must, usually long in advance. Check the Tabelog score beforehand, it changes.
en.baby_notes: Adults only dinner, in a room with 10 seats.
en.serves: Cha-kaiseki: kaiseki (a Japanese meal of many small dishes) in the style of a tea ceremony. Seasonal dishes come out one by one, with fish from the sea and rivers, in a delicate, clean taste.
en.todo: By reservation only and hard to get, so start early or ask the hotel. Late cancellation costs money.
en.special: One of the hardest tables to get in Kyoto, a counter with ten seats.
en.kosher_note: The meal is fixed and includes hamo (pike conger) and seafood. You can ask when booking for no pork or seafood, but they may not agree.
en.plan_line: Evening by booking only, closed 2nd and 4th Tue and Wed
en.baby_block: Long, quiet adults meal, not suitable for a baby

en.hype: Garlic ramen, and there's also a vegan bowl with soy protein that tastes like chicken thigh.
en.reality: The usual broth is pork tonkotsu, so you have to ask for the vegan bowl specifically.
en.tip: Order the vegan bowl and check with staff that it has no pork broth.
en.baby_notes: A small place with a counter, not comfortable for a stroller.
en.serves: Ramen with a lot of garlic. The regular version is in pork broth, and there's also a vegan version with soy protein.
en.kosher_note: Don't order the regular tonkotsu because the broth is pork, only the vegan or vegetarian bowl.
en.plan_line: Queue at lunch, come before opening or after 14:00
en.baby_block: Cramped, no stroller space, leave it outside

en.hype: Rare yakitori with Miyazaki Jitokko chicken, listed on Tabelog as a hidden place.
en.reality: Tabelog rating about 3.4, good but not outstanding.
en.tip: Take the course with the wine. Good for a quiet yakitori dinner.
en.plan_line: Book ahead, opens at 16:00 on weekends and holidays

en.hype: A tsukemen place that keeps popping up on ramen lists on TikTok and Instagram.
en.reality: On the Tabelog 100 six years in a row. The queue is the main problem.
en.tip: Come early or at quiet hours. There's only a counter of about 15 seats, so you queue on your own.
en.serves: Tsukemen: thick cold noodles you dip in a rich, thick fish and meat broth. At the end you can ask for hot soup to add to the broth and drink it.
en.todo: Buy a ticket from the machine at the entrance, it also has English. The queue is 20 minutes to an hour and a half but moves fast. Open 11:00–15:00 and 17:00–21:00, closed Sunday.
en.special: The broth is almost as thick as a sauce, and that's why people stand in line.
en.kosher_note: The broth is pork and fish based and comes with chashu, and there's no pork-free option.
en.plan_line: Cash only, no bookings. Best on weekday afternoons
en.baby_block: Basement stairs, hard with a stroller, and cramped

en.hype: A deli restaurant with Israeli and Jewish food.
en.reality: Average for the price.
en.tip: You can ask them for a Shabbat hotplate, so arrange it ahead.
en.baby_notes: A regular restaurant with no special queue, you can go in with a stroller and feed the baby.
en.serves: Israeli and Jewish deli food, like sandwiches and meat dishes.
en.kosher_note: Kosher supervision wasn't verified, ask by phone first.
en.plan_line: Shirokane. Call ahead, 03-5441-1211

en.hype: A small shrine close to Kyoto station, a calmer alternative to the famous Fushimi Inari gates.
en.reality: Quiet and less crowded than the main shrine.
en.tip: Good as a quiet stop before or after the main shrine. Check hours and how to get there first.
en.plan_line: Only worth it if you're already near the station

en.hype: A Buddhist temple cuisine restaurant, fully vegan with no animal products, with private rooms.
en.reality: A proper sit-down meal, fairly expensive.
en.tip: Ask for a private room when booking, then you can sit comfortably with the stroller.
en.baby_notes: The private rooms have space to feed and leave the stroller aside, but ask ahead whether the seating is on the floor.
en.serves: Buddhist temple cuisine (fucha ryori), entirely vegan. Lots of small dishes of vegetables, tofu and nuts.
en.kosher_note: Everything is vegan, so there's no meat, pork or seafood in the dishes.
en.plan_line: Booking only, closed Wednesdays and Thursdays
en.baby_block: Maybe tatami seating, not recommended without asking

en.hype: The department store where Kyotoites buy gifts and ready food in the basement.
en.reality: In the basement (depachika) it's easy to compare sweets, pickles and ready food in one place, without running between hundreds of shops. Open about 10:00–20:00, and year-end hours are unknown.
en.tip: Check the December hours on Daimaru's Japanese site. From November 2026 you pay full price and claim the tax refund at the airport on departure, so keep your passport and receipts.
en.baby_notes: There are lifts and probably a baby room, and you can eat and warm up without going out in the cold.
en.todo: Go down to the basement and loop through the sweets and wagashi of Kyoto shops, pickles and gift boxes. Buy small gifts for home and ready food for dinner. Then you can go up to the homeware and kitchen floors.
en.special: Many Kyoto shops in one heated place, handy when it's already dark by 16:30.
en.plan_line: Closes early on 31 Dec, and the basement is packed before New Year

en.hype: Specialises in oyakodon and chicken dishes, and the bowl there is excellent.
en.reality: Much pricier in the evening, and at lunch the price makes a lot more sense.
en.tip: Order the oyakodon, it's cheaper at lunch.
en.baby_notes: Floor seating on the second floor up stairs, not suitable for a stroller.
en.serves: Oyakodon is a rice bowl with chicken and soft egg in a slightly sweet sauce. The place also specialises in other chicken dishes.
en.kosher_note: Chicken, egg and rice, no pork or seafood.
en.plan_line: Closed Sundays and holidays, book ahead, check it's open at lunch
en.baby_block: Floor seating on the 2nd floor, stairs only

en.hype: One of the best Kobe beef restaurants in Tokyo.
en.reality: You need to book ahead, and the place suits a couple or a solo diner.
en.tip: Best to sit at the bar facing the chef.
en.baby_notes: Small bar facing the chef, no room for a stroller and the place suits a couple.
en.serves: Yakiniku is meat grilled over charcoal. Here it's quality Kobe beef that the chef prepares at the bar.
en.kosher_note: Beef, just make sure there's no pork in the sauces.
en.plan_line: Booking essential, best take the first seating at 17:00
en.baby_block: Small smoky bar, no stroller space

en.hype: A huge outlet with a view of Mount Fuji.
en.reality: There's a direct bus from Tokyo (for example from Shinjuku), about 1.5 hours and ¥1,600 to ¥2,200 each way. Worth it when you're in Tokyo, less so as a day trip from Osaka.
en.tip: Check the December bus timetables ahead, as they were updated in 2026. From November 2026 you pay full price and claim the tax refund at the airport on departure, so keep your passport and receipts.
en.baby_notes: The outlet is open air and easy with a stroller, but it's cold in December and you need to plan feeding breaks.
en.todo: Wander between the clothing and shoe brands, look at Fuji when it's clear, and finish before dark.
en.special: The best-known shopping destination in the area.
en.plan_line: Arrive at 10:00 before the crowds, closes at 19:00 in December

en.hype: A classic izakaya, you sit around the bar and order small dishes.
en.tip: Sit at the bar and order skewers and grilled fish.
en.baby_notes: A busy, crowded bar, not suitable for a stroller.
en.serves: A classic izakaya with a bar and seating around it. Meat skewers and grilled fish.
en.kosher_note: A lot of the skewers are pork, ask for chicken or fish with scales.
en.plan_line: Open daily from 10:00, no bookings, better outside peak hours
en.baby_block: Smoking inside and cramped, not suitable for a baby

en.hype: Kyoto's flagship fish ramen, number one in the Tabelog ramen ranking in Kyoto.
en.reality: The soup is clean and salty and the chashu is soft. Waiting is common, but worth it.
en.tip: 3 minutes' walk from Kawaramachi station. There are about 10 seats, so come early or at quiet hours. No takeaway noodles.
en.serves: Ramen with a clear, deep fish broth with a taste of bonito flakes. Light with white soy sauce or dark with dark soy sauce, topped with chashu (soft pork), and you can add an egg.
en.todo: The place is small and there's always a queue, and at peak hours you may wait 45 minutes. There's also another branch called Hanare, so check the current address.
en.special: Considered Kyoto's most famous fish ramen, with a Michelin Bib Gourmand.
en.kosher_note: The broth is fish and that's good, but it's served with pork chashu, so ask for no chashu and check there's no pork fat.
en.plan_line: Closed Wed, arrive 30 min before opening or book a month ahead
en.baby_block: Small, counter only, no stroller space

en.hype: A basement lane of famous ramen shops inside Tokyo station.
en.reality: The quality is good and the atmosphere is fun. It feels touristy, but the bowls are better than they look.
en.tip: A handy stop if you're passing through Tokyo station. Pick a shop with a short queue.
en.serves: Several well-known ramen shops in the station basement. There's tsukemen (noodles you dip in a strong, thick broth) and ramen in a seafood and pork broth, and most dishes have pork or chicken.
dishes: Seafood and pork ramen at Ikaruga
en.todo: Each shop has a ticket machine at the entrance, and sometimes you pay before the queue and sometimes after, so look at the sign. Credit cards don't work, only cash or an IC card. Rokurinsha has a long queue but it moves fast.
en.special: Several of the city's big ramen shops in one place, and the favourite of them all is Rokurinsha with its dipping noodles.
en.kosher_note: Most broths are pork or seafood based. You can look for shoyu in chicken broth, but you have to ask at each shop.
en.plan_line: Queue of 30–60 minutes, best before 11:00 or after 14:00
en.baby_block: Small shops and a standing queue, no stroller space

en.hype: Osaka's famous whisky and cocktail bar, known for precise classics.
en.reality: People praise the bartender's cocktails, but the service isn't always consistent.
en.tip: Only five seats. Open Monday to Saturday 18:00–00:00, and ask the bartender for a classic.
en.baby_notes: Adults only: a tiny bar with five seats, late evening, no room for a stroller.
en.serves: A cocktail and whisky bar in Osaka. They make classics like a martini and an old fashioned precisely, and there's a selection of Japanese whisky. There's no kitchen, so you come for the drinks.
en.todo: An evening bar in the Kitashinchi area, quiet and for adults. Check hours and booking first.
en.special: Appears again and again in Asia's 50 Best, and is ranked on the Tabelog Bar 100 (number 40, score 3.7 in 2022).
en.kosher_note: A cocktail and whisky bar with no kitchen, you can order anything.
en.plan_line: Book and arrive after 20:00, closed Sunday
en.baby_block: Small night bar, not suitable for a baby

en.hype: A flat walk from Kyoto station that's easy with a stroller, and a relaxed outing for babies.
en.reality: A barrier-free building with ramps and lifts.
en.tip: Walk from Kyoto station along the tracks, it's flat. Check the official site for the dolphin show and stroller rental.
en.baby_notes: 2–3 nursing rooms, several changing tables and free stroller parking.
en.price: Paid entry, check the baby price on the official site.
en.todo: Walk between the tanks: the great ocean, Japan's rivers and forests, penguins and seals, and Kyoto's water life. There are lifts between floors. There's also a dolphin stadium.
en.special: Japanese river life, including the giant salamander you see up close, and everything is air-conditioned and near the station.
en.plan_line: Tickets online, arrive at opening, open at year end too

en.hype: Fluffy pancakes that made it onto Tokyo's must-do lists.
en.reality: There's usually a queue.
en.tip: Order the classic pancake with butter and maple.
en.baby_notes: A small place with a queue, no proper space for a stroller.
en.serves: Japanese soufflé-style pancakes, very fluffy and soft. Served with butter and maple or with fruit and cream.
en.kosher_note: The pancakes have no meat or fish. Avoid dishes with bacon.
en.plan_line: Pancakes take 20 minutes; come at opening or book online

en.hype: Considered one of the most beautiful bookshops in the world.
en.reality: The design is impressive: three connected buildings, books on design and architecture, and a cafe. A bit pricey, and more about the atmosphere than shopping.
en.tip: Come in the morning when it's quiet and then carry on to the lanes of Daikanyama. Check the hours on the site first.
en.baby_notes: Most of the building is on one floor with wide aisles, usually easy with a stroller, and the neighbourhood is quiet.
en.todo: Browse the books on design and food, then have coffee and read. After that walk to the boutiques and small shops in the neighbourhood.
en.special: A bookshop that is also a design space: art and architecture books, magazines and music in one place.
en.plan_line: Open until 02:00, you can sit in the cafe among the books

en.hype: The omakase sushi restaurant at the top of Tokyo's must-do lists.
en.reality: Almost impossible to book as a tourist, and the price is very high.
en.tip: Ask the concierge at a luxury hotel to check availability months ahead.
en.baby_notes: A very small place with a counter, no room for a stroller, a short quiet meal that doesn't suit a baby.
en.serves: Sushi omakase: the chef chooses and serves piece after piece. All fish and seafood on rice.
en.kosher_note: The sushi is the chef's choice and includes seafood, it can't be adjusted.
en.plan_line: Via hotel concierge only, closed Sunday and Saturday evening
en.baby_block: 10-seat basement sushi counter, not suitable for a baby

en.hype: The twin-tower building with a roof garden and 360 degree view, one of the most photographed spots in Osaka.
en.reality: Best around sunset, and there are long queues at peak hours.
en.tip: Come about an hour before sunset, leave hats and umbrellas, and check the official price first.
en.todo: Go up in a glass lift and then on escalators in a glass tube between the two towers, up to the 39th floor, about 170 metres high. At the top there's an open deck all round with a 360° view of Osaka, and inside a cafe and a shop. The deck closes in strong wind, and in December it's very cold there.
en.special: Two towers joined at the top like a gate, with an escalator tube hanging in the air between them.
en.plan_line: Book your ticket online, the queue at the desk is the slow part

en.hype: A cafe with a window seat where you watch deer wander by while drinking a matcha latte.
en.reality: A known deer-watching spot, and busy on weekends.
en.tip: Order a matcha latte and the hojicha sweets, and ask for a table by the window.
en.serves: A cafe with a window overlooking the deer of Nara Park. Order a hot matcha latte or a sweet drink and sit by the window.
en.todo: It's in demand, especially on weekends, so come early or midweek. There's no info on reserving a seat, you probably just go in and wait for a window table.
en.special: You drink while deer wander past the window, and with a baby it's pleasant because you sit inside in the warm.
en.kosher_note: Hot and sweet drinks, no pork or seafood.
en.plan_line: Confirm the address first, the cafe is in town, not inside the park
en.baby_block: Narrow entrance and upper floor, hard with a stroller

en.hype: Grill fish and seafood yourselves at the table, and fried shrimp you can't miss.
en.reality: A noisy izakaya.
en.tip: Order the fried shrimp and cheap beer or sake.
en.baby_notes: Smoke and tight seating, not for a baby.
en.serves: An izakaya is a Japanese bar with small dishes. Here you grill fish and seafood yourselves on a table grill.
en.kosher_note: The place is built on seafood. There are fish with scales, but most of it isn't suitable.
en.plan_line: Better to book for the evening
en.baby_block: Smoking possible inside, check when booking

en.hype: A year-end flea market in the temple grounds, with about a thousand stalls.
en.reality: This is the last Kobo-san of the year. There are antiques, second-hand clothes, homeware and New Year items, but also a huge crowd.
en.tip: Come in the morning, about 8–11, when it's easy to wander and the choice is full, and bring cash.
en.baby_notes: Heavy crowds and gravel in parts of the grounds, a carrier is better than a stroller, and if your baby doesn't like commotion, skip it.
en.todo: Arrive early and wander between stalls of old ceramics, fabrics and second-hand kimono. You can also buy New Year decorations and food from the stalls. At the end go into the temple grounds and the pagoda.
en.special: A chance to feel the Japanese year end with the locals, who come to shop for New Year.
en.plan_line: The market is only on 21 December 2026, a Monday
en.baby_block: Very crowded, hard with a stroller, carrier better

en.hype: A quiet temple in the hills, an alternative to Tofuku-ji.
en.reality: Without a big crowd.
en.tip: Come early in the morning.
en.plan_line: Closes at 16:30 in December, last entry 16:00

en.hype: The tallest tower in Japan, and the standard photo of every first-time visitor.
en.reality: Long queues and a high entry price, and there are cheaper observation decks with a similar view.
en.tip: You can skip it unless you really want the glass floor. The free roof of the city hall building in Shinjuku gives a similar view.
en.plan_line: Timed ticket on the site, go up toward sunset (~16:30)

en.hype: A secluded bamboo grove on the temple paths that few people know about.
en.reality: At midday it can be almost empty, but there's no guarantee.
en.tip: Walk the paths around the temple and not only the main hall, and come early to enjoy the grove in peace.
en.price: The temple grounds cost money, about ¥700 (check)
en.todo: Enter the Zen temple in Higashiyama and wander between the gardens, the pond and the tea houses. Carry on along the paths that go round the main hall to the bamboo grove. You can combine it with the old streets nearby, Ninenzaka and Sannenzaka.
en.special: The grove is small and quiet, different from the dense Arashiyama grove, and the temple itself was founded in 1606.
en.plan_line: Last entry 17:00, open in the evening too until 13 December
en.baby_block: Stairs and paths, hard with a stroller

en.hype: Famous tonkatsu with soft pork cutlets and fillet cutlet sandwiches.
en.reality: Tabelog rating about 3.45 from around 1,200–1,500 reviews. The cutlets are crisp and juicy, the price is premium and the service isn't always consistent.
en.tip: Lunch sets are the best value. If you want the signature dish, the fillet sandwich.
en.plan_line: Come before 12:00 or after 14:00 to skip the lunch queue

en.hype: A small, cheap cafe and dessert place, away from the tourist routes.
en.reality: Tabelog score about 3.75. Simple and compact, coffee and cakes without fuss or show.
en.tip: Good for a dessert stop between exploring Ueno and Yushima shrine.
en.serves: A small cafe near Yushima that lives on good coffee and cake. Order a cup of coffee and a slice, no trends.
en.todo: Walk in and sit down, no booking and probably no queue. The place is small, so with a stroller check there's room.
en.special: A quiet corner away from the tourist routes.
en.kosher_note: Coffee and cake, no pork or seafood.
en.plan_line: Come early, the cakes run out in the afternoon, especially on weekends

en.hype: A lantern-lit stone lane with over 60 izakayas and bars near Dotonbori.
en.reality: Atmospheric and popular with locals too, but many tourist places. A small bar beats the big names.
en.tip: Come around 18:00–20:00 before it fills up, and go into a small izakaya or a standing bar.
en.serves: A narrow stone lane with dozens of izakayas (small Japanese pubs) and bars. They serve small plates like skewers with beer or sake.
en.todo: There's no single queue, just pick a small bar and walk in. Prices depend on the place, and some charge a cover fee. With a baby, come early.
en.special: The Fudo Myoo shrine inside the lane, where you splash water on the statue for luck, and the mood is calmer than Dotonbori.
en.kosher_note: There's a lot of pork and seafood, choose chicken or vegetable skewers and ask everywhere before ordering.
en.plan_line: Prettiest after dark
en.baby_block: Narrow lane with stone steps, hard with a stroller

en.hype: Top-level tempura, on the list of Tokyo's must-visit restaurants.
en.reality: Hard to get a seat and the price is high, especially in the evening.
en.tip: Book lunch if you can, it's cheaper and the tempura is the same quality.
en.baby_notes: A small place with a counter and no room for a stroller, a quiet meal that doesn't suit a baby.
en.serves: Tempura is vegetables and fish in a light batter, fried in front of you and served hot, piece by piece. The focus is on seasonal vegetables like sweet potato.
en.kosher_note: Vegetables are the stars, like the famous sweet potato, and there's fish too. Ask when booking for no shrimp or seafood.
en.plan_line: Closed Sundays, book months ahead
en.baby_block: Upscale 20-seat counter, not suitable for a baby

en.hype: A German-style Christmas market at the foot of the Umeda Sky towers.
en.reality: Entry is free, and it's more about atmosphere, food and drinks than shopping. In 2026 it runs from 13 November.
en.tip: Go after about 17:00, when the lights really show. Check stalls and hours on the official site.
en.baby_notes: The area is open and easy with a stroller, but it's cold in the evening, so dress warm.
en.todo: Wander between the stalls in Wonder Square, drink something hot and see the 25-metre LED tree. You can add a trip up to the observatory on the 40th floor.
en.special: A European holiday market with a giant tree beneath one of Osaka's best-known buildings.
en.plan_line: Runs only until 25 Dec

en.hype: A small bar down an alley in Ebisu, with absinthe and herbal liqueurs, forgotten classics and original cocktails.
en.reality: 4.7 on Google from about 700 reviews. People praise the cocktails, the attentive bartenders and the intimate mood.
en.tip: Ask the bartender for an absinthe drink or an off-menu classic.
en.baby_notes: A small, intimate bar with an adult crowd, not for a baby.
en.serves: A small bar in an Ebisu alley, all absinthe and herbal liqueurs like Chartreuse. The menu runs from light to strong cocktails, and if you don't know what to pick you can ask the bartender.
en.todo: The bar doesn't take reservations, so just turn up and wait for a table. Open in the evening, roughly 19:00 to 02:00. There may be a cover charge (it used to be 500 yen), and there's no real food.
en.special: Running since 2010, with one of the more serious absinthe selections in Tokyo.
en.kosher_note: A cocktail and absinthe bar, no problem, you just order drinks.
en.plan_line: No bookings, best to arrive right at opening
en.baby_block: Small adults' bar, not suitable for a baby

en.hype: Clear, clean and cheap ramen.
en.reality: A small place, open only in the morning and at lunch, with a queue at peak hours.
en.tip: Order the regular ramen in the clear broth.
en.baby_notes: A small, cramped counter with no room for a stroller, better for a couple without the baby.
en.serves: Shoyu (soy sauce) ramen in a clear, light broth, with thin noodles and simple toppings. The broth is usually chicken, dried fish and pork.
en.kosher_note: The broth and the standard topping are built on pork and dried fish, so there's almost nothing to choose.
en.plan_line: Arrive before opening, the place is tiny
en.baby_block: Tiny place with a queue outside, hard with a stroller

en.hype: The open-air roof of Shibuya Scramble Square is Tokyo's best-known viewpoint, and it's in every best-views reel.
en.reality: The view is excellent, but sunset tickets sell out within minutes.
en.tip: Pick a clear day and dress in layers, because December is cold and windy and sunset is around 16:30. If it's cloudy, skip it, the free roof of the Shinjuku city hall building is a cheap backup.
en.todo: Take the lift up the top floors of Shibuya Scramble Square and step out onto an open roof about 230 metres high. Walk the deck with a 360° view over the crossing and all of Tokyo, and on a clear day you can see Fuji too. There's a glass corner for photos and a spot with hammocks.
en.special: A truly open roof with no glass in the way, and from the top you see the most famous crossing in the world.
en.plan_line: Buy the sunset ticket the moment sales open, 20-minute entry window

en.hype: A street of Japanese knives, kitchenware and plastic food you can't find anywhere else.
en.reality: One of the best places in Tokyo for kitchenware, especially knives. The street is long with lots of specialist shops, and locals and chefs really shop there.
en.tip: Knives can be engraved with a name, and you pack them in your checked suitcase.
en.baby_notes: The pavements are wide and easy with a stroller, but the shops are narrow with sharp objects, so better to stay outside.
en.todo: Walk along the street and go into the knife, ceramics and pan shops. At the end buy a souvenir like tableware or plastic food.
en.special: Knife shops where the sellers help you choose a knife by the kind of cutting, everything a pro kitchen needs in one place.
en.plan_line: Most shops closed Sundays and holidays, come on a weekday before 17:00

en.hype: An old stall, open from early morning, with rice and a simple, very tasty beef stew.
en.reality: In tourist season the queue can be at least an hour, sometimes much more.
en.tip: If you survived the queue, add a soft egg and skip the offal dish.
en.baby_notes: A small stall with a long queue outside, not practical with a stroller.
en.serves: Gyudon is a rice bowl with beef and onion simmered in sweet soy sauce. Classic and simple.
en.kosher_note: Beef on rice with no pork, don't order the offal dish.
en.plan_line: Queue before opening, closed Sundays, Wednesdays and holidays
en.baby_block: Small counter with a long queue, no stroller space

en.hype: The giant mechanical crab sign is one of the most photographed spots in Osaka.
en.reality: Touristy and pricey, and the service isn't always polite. The portions are good, but it's mainly a landmark, not what locals choose.
en.tip: Photograph the sign and eat crab somewhere cheaper.
en.plan_line: Book a table ahead on the site; lunch set is much cheaper than dinner

en.hype: Vegan ramen that people keep coming back to.
en.reality: There's a queue.
en.tip: It's in Parco.
en.baby_notes: A small place with a queue, not much room for a stroller.
en.serves: Vegan ramen in a big bowl, with a rich broth with no meat and no fish.
en.kosher_note: The vegan ramen has no pork or seafood.
en.plan_line: Arrive before 12:00 or after 14:00 to beat the queue

en.hype: A huge open park with a giant slide and a soft-floor play area, good for an active family day.
en.reality: You can rent strollers on site.
en.tip: Bring a picnic and a light stroller for the grass areas.
en.baby_notes: Five nursing rooms, four in the Japanese garden and one in the nature and cultural gardens. The Moricara nature hall has a kids' space and a nursing room.
en.price: Entry to the park and most areas is free, and some attractions charge a small fee.
en.todo: A huge park in north Osaka, on the site of the 1970 expo. Go see the Tower of the Sun, continue to the Japanese garden and the nature and cultural gardens, and finish on the grass or in the Wakuwaku Pond soft play area.
en.special: Taro Okamoto's giant Tower of the Sun statue remains from the 1970 World Expo and became a symbol.
en.plan_line: Closed Wednesdays and 28 Dec to 1 Jan, last entry 16:30

en.hype: Osaka's famous kitchen market, with grilled wagyu skewers and seafood stalls, packed with tourists.
en.reality: Prices are inflated for tourists, especially for seafood and Kobe beef. The freshness and food are good, but many think the tourist markup isn't worth it.
en.tip: Try a few bites from the stalls rather than sitting down for a meal. Skip the pricey seafood, and for cheaper sushi go to Kizu market.
en.plan_line: Come in the morning hungry and with cash, very busy 28–31 Dec

en.hype: A regular spot for udon, cheap and tasty, with thick noodles soft as clouds.
en.reality: Small, and at busy times there's a queue that moves fast.
en.tip: Order a basic udon, hot or cold, it's the best one with no odd toppings.
en.baby_notes: A small, busy place with tight seating, not suitable for a stroller.
en.serves: Udon is thick, soft wheat noodles, here Sanuki style. Served in hot broth or cold with a sauce on the side, and you can add butter or fish roe.
en.kosher_note: The broth is dried bonito fish, which is fine. A plain hot or cold bowl works, just skip the fish roe and the shrimp.
en.plan_line: Closes when the dough runs out, better to come early
en.baby_block: Small and cramped, not suitable for a stroller

en.hype: An 800-metre covered pedestrian street where Kyoto residents do their everyday shopping.
en.reality: One of the biggest covered streets in western Japan, with lots of locals and few tourists, including a popular bakery and tofu shop. No polished souvenirs.
en.tip: Come at lunchtime or early afternoon, before it gets dark at 16:30.
en.baby_notes: Covered, flat and quiet, good for a stroller and a baby break.
en.todo: Wander the street, buy a pastry, tofu or a sweet from local shops, and see what Kyoto looks like without tourists. You can combine it with nearby Nijo Castle.
en.special: Everyday Kyoto life rather than tourism, at lower prices than the centre.
en.plan_line: Year-end hours unknown, check first
en.baby_block: Bikes and cars till 14:00, hard with a stroller

en.hype: A small sushi counter in Kitashinchi, a quiet, serious evening in the Edomae style.
en.reality: Tabelog score 4.09, and chosen for the 2025 Sushi WEST 100.
en.tip: Bookings are through Tabelog. Confirm the current number of seats and price when you book.
en.baby_notes: Adults only, small seating, not suitable for a stroller or a 5-month-old baby.
en.price: Unknown, budget for a full omakase evening
en.serves: Edomae-style sushi (the classic Tokyo style, fish on gently seasoned rice) at a small counter. The chef makes each nigiri in front of you by season, and hands it straight to your hand or plate.
en.todo: Book ahead, and there's no official price, so check first. Similar sushi restaurants in Kitashinchi cost 30,000 yen and up, which is only a guide. Open in the evening only, 18:00–23:00.
en.special: A small counter of 7–8 seats, quiet, serious and focused on the food.
en.kosher_note: Lots of shrimp, shellfish and caviar. When booking, ask for only fish with scales such as tuna, salmon and sea bream.
en.plan_line: Booking essential, closed Sundays
en.baby_block: Small 7–8 seat counter, no stroller space

en.hype: Matcha-flavoured shaved ice loaded with toppings, for matcha lovers.
en.reality: The dessert is big and relatively pricey, and there's usually a queue.
en.tip: Order one ice dessert and share it.
en.baby_notes: A small place with tight seating, no room for a stroller.
en.serves: Kakigori, finely shaved matcha-flavoured ice with sauces and toppings.
en.kosher_note: Ice and matcha dessert, no pork or seafood.
en.plan_line: Open daily, small place, best to come midday
en.baby_block: Tiny place with about 6 seats, hard with a stroller

en.hype: An elegant port city with high-end shopping.
en.reality: From Osaka Station about 20–25 minutes on the JR, for ¥410. Motomachi is a covered arcade with boutiques, craft shops and second-hand. A nice day, not an impressive shopping destination.
en.tip: Start in the morning at Kitano or Sannomiya and walk down through Motomachi to the harbour, so it's all downhill.
en.baby_notes: The arcade is covered and flat and good for a stroller, but the climb to Kitano isn't easy.
en.todo: Get off at Sannomiya, walk to Motomachi for the boutiques and craft shops, stop in Nankinmachi and finish at Harborland and the harbour at sunset, around 16:45 in December.
en.special: Shopping and a harbour view on the same day, and calmer than Osaka.
en.plan_line: Check ahead the hours and closing days of shops you want

en.hype: Casual, cheap sushi of much higher quality than its category, a good place to start.
en.reality: Long queues at mealtimes, and sometimes you wait a long time.
en.tip: Come just before or after lunch, and take a queue number from the machine first.
en.baby_notes: There are regular tables too, not only a counter, but the queue is long and it's tight for a stroller.
en.serves: Casual sushi with big nigiri and lots of fish, and a wide choice even if you don't eat raw fish.
en.kosher_note: Choose salmon, tuna, sea bream and yellowtail, and skip shrimp, octopus, squid, sea urchin and shellfish.
en.plan_line: Book on TableCheck, without a booking the queue can reach an hour

en.hype: The heart-shaped window in the guest hall that frames the garden, a favourite on Instagram and blogs.
en.reality: A small, quiet place, and the window is the main draw. Hours and bus routes change, so check first.
en.tip: Go right after opening or near closing, for soft light and fewer people. The heart shadow only appears on the right day. Take the bus to Ichu-mae and then a taxi from Uji.
en.todo: Travel from Uji or Kyoto to a small mountain village and enter a quiet Buddhist temple. Sit on the mats in the guest hall facing the heart window (inome) that frames the garden, and take photos. Then stroll the garden and courtyard.
en.special: A small, quiet place away from Kyoto's crowds, but not easy to get to.
highlights: Heart window in the guest hall
en.plan_line: Open to the public until 6 Dec, closed on your trip dates
en.baby_block: Children under school age not allowed

en.hype: A famous kaiseki name in Kyoto, with Michelin stars and dishes served like a picture.
en.reality: Flawless service and menu explanations in English. One review found the price hard to justify and the service not at Michelin level.
en.tip: Think of it as the one splurge meal of the trip, and come only if you want a formal kaiseki evening.
en.serves: Kyoto kaiseki: a seasonal meal of many small dishes in pottery. Sashimi, fish, vegetables and a clear soup, and each dish is presented like a picture.
en.todo: Booking ahead is a must, one to three months, and the hotel concierge can help. Lunch starts at about 22,000 yen, and dinner costs more. Ask ahead whether you sit on a cushion or on a chair.
en.special: One of the best-known kaiseki names in Kyoto, with Michelin stars.
en.kosher_note: Fixed kaiseki with seafood. You can ask when booking for no pork or seafood, but there's no promise.
en.plan_line: Book months ahead, closed at year end
en.baby_block: Ask ahead, babies not recommended unless they agree

en.hype: Shirasu omelette, strawberry mochi and gold-leaf ice cream, all on one street near Kamakura station.
en.reality: The stalls on the main street are the most touristy, and the better food is on the side streets.
en.tip: Eat at Hannari Inari or another shop a block or two off the main street.
en.plan_line: Red gate by the station; weekends too packed for strollers

en.hype: Clear shoyu chinten ramen.
en.plan_line: The Brick Square branch, come before opening

en.hype: Kitchen knives of Kyoto chefs, from a shop with centuries of history inside Nishiki Market.
en.reality: The knives are really good, but the shop is touristy and crowded. Prices start around ¥10,000 and quickly climb past ¥50,000.
en.tip: Engraving is free, so buy one good knife rather than several. On a flight the knife has to go in checked luggage.
en.baby_notes: The shop is narrow inside a crowded market, so better to take turns and not go in with the stroller.
en.todo: Go in, ask for an explanation of the knife types and choose one for everyday use, like a Santoku. Ask for a name engraving and wait a few minutes. The knife is packed in a box ready for the flight.
en.special: One purchase you use for years instead of another souvenir, and the engraving makes it yours.
en.plan_line: Engraving takes a few minutes, do it before your other shopping

en.hype: Kyoto's best-known matcha spot on Instagram: matcha tiramisu in a hinoki wood box, with about 1.2 million views online.
en.reality: Popular and no secret, so expect a big crowd on Ninenzaka. Pretty, but more about the photo than a special matcha dessert.
en.tip: Better matcha at GOKAGO or Kasagiya, without the Ninenzaka crowd. Skip the queue here.
en.plan_line: Arrive at opening at 10:00, the queue is long in the afternoon

en.hype: A kaiseki-style lunch in the Kiyomizu area.
en.reality: Reviews are mixed. On one side a tourist trap with dishes that weren't always what was ordered, on the other a bonito sashimi that got praise.
en.tip: Better to skip it, unless you can check the menu and be sure what you're ordering. Similar dishes at a fair price are at a local obanzai place.
en.plan_line: Book an evening table ahead

en.hype: Street touts pull tourists into bars for a light evening of entertainment, and in vlogs it looks fun.
en.reality: There are reports of bills around 50,000 yen, with an entry fee, a fixed table charge and snacks nobody ordered.
en.tip: Ask for a written price list in English before you order, and walk away if the bill looks wrong.
en.plan_line: Don't follow the touts on the street
en.baby_block: Adults only cabaret bars, smoking inside

en.hype: Famous for its autumn colours and the Tsutenkyo bridge.
en.reality: In autumn it's packed to the brim, with crowds like a rush hour. There may also be a quieter bamboo path.
en.tip: Come early and avoid weekends at peak leaf season. The wide grounds are free.
en.todo: Walk around a big Zen temple complex in south Kyoto, pass through the huge Sanmon gate and enter the Hojo gardens with the modern Zen garden that looks like a chessboard of moss and stone. You also cross the Tsutenkyo bridge over the valley. That part is paid.
en.special: Shigemori Mirei's modern Zen garden and the maple valley under the bridge. In December most of the leaves have fallen, but there's far less of a crowd.
en.plan_line: Arrive at 9:00 opening and finish before 15:30, entry closes early

en.hype: A smoky yakitori alley north of Shinjuku station, the classic TikTok night spot.
en.reality: Tiny bars with 6–8 seats. Some places are touristy, but the atmosphere is real.
en.tip: Bring cash, and remember a group of four usually has to split between two places.
en.serves: A narrow, smoky alley next to the station, full of tiny bars grilling yakitori, chicken skewers on a charcoal grill. You order skewer after skewer, of chicken and offal, with beer or a highball (whisky and soda).
en.todo: Turn up, peek in and go into a place with a free seat, no booking. There's almost always smoke, so with a baby just pass through for a moment, or one couple goes without the baby.
en.special: An alley that's been there since about 1947 with real atmosphere, and Torien and Fukuhachi are long-time picks.
en.kosher_note: Chicken yakitori works, but many stalls serve pork skewers and offal, so choose only chicken and vegetables.
en.plan_line: Arrive before 18:00 to get a spot at the counter
en.baby_block: Bar smoke, cramped, sometimes stairs, no stroller

en.hype: A shopping centre in the original post office building near Tokyo station, with a view of the station.
en.reality: Japanese designer clothes and regional food products from all over Japan. The shops aren't very unique, but the location is handy and the December mood is good.
en.tip: Come before sunset, around 16:30, and then see the lights on Marunouchi Nakadori. The 2026 light-up dates are unknown.
en.baby_notes: A modern place with lifts and wide aisles, easy with a stroller.
en.todo: Go into KITTE, wander the souvenir shops and go up to the garden on the 6th floor for photos of the station. Then go out to the lit avenue and finish by walking along Nakadori.
en.special: The building is Tokyo's historic central post office, and it has a market of regional products from all over Japan.
en.plan_line: Open until 21:00, expect short hours on 31 Dec

en.hype: Contemporary art on the 53rd floor of Mori Tower, with a panoramic view of Tokyo.
en.reality: A smart choice for art with a view, without the queues of the big attractions.
en.tip: Come at sunset for the view.
en.todo: Go up Mori Tower in Roppongi to the top floors (52–53) and see changing contemporary art exhibitions. Then look out over Tokyo from the big windows. You can add Tokyo City View, the observation deck in the same building, on a joint or separate ticket.
en.special: A contemporary art museum on the 53rd floor, so one visit gives you art and a view, and the exhibitions change.
en.plan_line: Tuesdays it closes at 17:00, check hours in late December

en.hype: A small sake bar whose owner was born in Israel, maybe a fun fit for the group.
en.reality: An old, huge sake list, and the owner matches sake to everyone's taste. Tabelog score 3.52, and some think the owner is condescending.
en.tip: A tiny bar with 9–10 seats. You come for the personal sake matching, not for a meal.
en.baby_notes: A drinking-only bar with a tiny room, late hours, adults only.
en.serves: A tiny sake bar in an old wooden house, with a long list including aged sake (koshu, deep and slightly sweet). Yoram, the owner, asks what you like and pours what suits, and there's no real food menu.
en.todo: Cash only. Four drinks come to about 4,000 yen. One site says the bar is temporarily closed, so call first.
en.special: The owner is an Israeli who has lived in Japan for years, knows the sake world from the inside, and you can talk to him in Hebrew.
en.kosher_note: A sake bar with no kitchen, you drink sake and it's no problem.
en.plan_line: Open Wednesday to Saturday, 18:00–00:00
en.baby_block: Tiny bar with no stroller space, not suitable for a baby

en.hype: Matcha gelato in different strength levels.
en.reality: There's a queue at busy times, and the portion is sometimes small for the price.
en.tip: Start at a medium level and work up. The strongest level is very bitter.
en.baby_notes: You can take it in a cup and eat by the stroller, and the place is near Sensoji.
en.serves: Japanese green tea gelato in seven strength levels, from delicate to very bitter and strong. Served in a cup or a cone.
en.kosher_note: Milk and tea based gelato, no meat or fish.
en.plan_line: Closes at 17:00, and there's a queue on weekends

en.hype: A ten-seat tempura counter that ranks high on tempura lists.
en.reality: Tabelog score about 4.5. It's unclear whether the award is Gold or Silver.
en.tip: Judge by the current Tabelog page, not by award claims.
en.baby_notes: A ten-seat counter by booking only, adults only, no space for kids or a stroller.
en.serves: A small counter of about ten seats, where the chef fries tempura (fish and vegetables in a thin, crisp batter) and serves it piece by piece, hot from the oil. Expect seafood, shrimp and seasonal vegetables, and usually rice at the end.
en.todo: By reservation only, and sometimes you need a referral or the hotel concierge. Find out the price first.
en.special: One of the highest-ranked tempura counters in Tokyo, almost like eating at the chef's living room.
en.kosher_note: Fixed course with shrimp and seafood, ask when booking to swap them for fish and vegetables.
en.plan_line: Hard to get a seat, book through a concierge months ahead
en.baby_block: Quiet 2nd-floor counter, adults only

en.hype: A seafood izakaya and sake bar, a short walk from Fukushima station (Hanshin), with a second branch for groups.
en.reality: Tabelog score 3.53, but there's little information about the place.
en.tip: The address is Fukushima 1-3-16. Groups of up to 40 can use the second branch. Check Tabelog for hours and booking.
en.baby_notes: A sake-focused izakaya, probably adults only.
en.serves: An izakaya (a Japanese bar with small food and drinks) with fresh fish and seafood and creative dishes, like anko (monkfish) in tomato sauce, cream croquettes and crispy roast chicken. Order a few dishes for the table and share, with sake.
en.todo: Order several dishes to share, tapas style. The dish names here are unofficial, and there's no price info.
en.special: A neighbourhood place, not touristy, close to the station.
en.kosher_note: The focus is seafood, including anko, which isn't a fish with scales. You can get by with the roast chicken and croquettes, but the choice is limited.
en.plan_line: Better to book a table ahead
en.baby_block: Sake izakaya, adults only

en.hype: A small six-seat cocktail room, with an entrance that's hard to spot.
en.reality: 4.6 on Google from 140 reviews, check the current number.
en.tip: Come early in the evening.
en.baby_notes: Adults only: six seats, no baby facilities.
en.serves: A small basement cocktail bar with a seasonal menu. The bartender Ryu Fujii tweaks classics a little, and he's also known for alcohol-free cocktails.
en.todo: The entrance is on basement level 2 of the Osaka Ekimae Daiichi building, with a small sign that's easy to miss. There's no clear info on reservations, so call or message them on Instagram. There's probably also a small cover charge.
en.special: The first Osaka bar to enter Asia's 50 Best Bars, number 28 in 2024 and 58 in 2025.
en.kosher_note: A cocktail bar, even alcohol-free, no problem.
en.plan_line: Better to book, closed Sundays
en.baby_block: Small adults' bar, 6 seats, not suitable for a baby

en.hype: Unlike the tourist traps in the area: excellent fish, a careful atmosphere and a low price for what you get.
en.reality: Around Tsukiji market there are queues, and at peak hours you wait.
en.tip: Come early to beat the queue, and order the nigiri set.
en.baby_notes: Counter seating in a small space, no room for a stroller.
en.serves: A sushi shop near Tsukiji market with fresh fish from the market, served as nigiri and sets at a reasonable price.
en.kosher_note: Choose tuna, salmon, sea bream and yellowtail, and skip shrimp, octopus, squid, shellfish, sea urchin and eel.
en.plan_line: Check hours on maps, Tsukiji shops close on Wednesdays

en.hype: Hidden alleys with hundreds of tiny izakayas that tourists barely find.
en.reality: The alleys are used mostly by local workers, with no signs for tourists. In many places the menu is in Japanese only and there's no online booking.
en.tip: Pick a place on Tabelog and go on a weekday evening. You can also take a guided izakaya tour if you want help ordering.
en.serves: An izakaya is a small Japanese pub, and in the alleys behind Tenmangu shrine there are hundreds. You eat yakitori (chicken skewers on a grill) and small dishes to share, with beer or sake.
en.todo: There's no one place to recommend, just go into one that looks good. Many of the places are small and full of smoke.
en.special: Not one place but a whole neighbourhood of local workers, with a real Osaka evening atmosphere.
en.kosher_note: Chicken skewers, grilled vegetables and salads are fine, but some places also have pork belly and shrimp, ask before ordering.
en.plan_line: Cash only and Japanese menus, bring a translation app
en.baby_block: Narrow alleys and cramped places, some smoking

en.hype: A crisp beef cutlet with a famous queue, loved in Instagram and TikTok videos.
en.reality: Excellent value for the quality, with a wait of 20 minutes or more at peak hours.
en.tip: If the queue is long, ask the staff about the nearby branches.
en.serves: Gyukatsu: breaded beef slices fried briefly, pink inside. They arrive with a hot stone, and you sear each slice for a few seconds as you like. Comes with rice, soup, shredded cabbage and sauces.
en.todo: At busy times you wait 20 minutes or more, and you order while in the queue. A small set costs about 1,900–2,500 yen, check whether it's cash only. You can also book on TableCheck.
en.special: One of the best-known gyukatsu chains, with good value, and half the fun is searing it yourselves on the stone.
en.kosher_note: Beef cutlet you sear yourselves on a stone, with rice, cabbage and miso soup, no pork or seafood.
en.plan_line: Arrive about 20 minutes before opening, no advance booking
en.baby_block: In a basement, probably hard with a stroller

en.hype: Big lawns and flat paths, a favourite for a picnic with small kids.
en.reality: Flat paths and big lawns. Check the opening hours.
en.tip: Come early to borrow a stroller. You can bring your own food for a picnic, alcohol is not allowed.
en.baby_notes: Strollers are loaned at every gate with no booking, nursing rooms near Kitayama Gate and in the botanical garden hall, changing tables and shaded lawns.
en.todo: Stroll the wide, flat paths between big lawns, flower gardens and wooded areas. There's a big greenhouse with tropical plants, a nice place to warm up on a cold December day. You can have a picnic on the grass.
en.special: Japan's oldest public botanical garden, from 1924, quiet and much more open than Kyoto's tourist sites.
highlights: Strollers to borrow at the gates
en.plan_line: The gardens are closed 28 Dec to 4 Jan

en.hype: High-end yakiniku, on the list of Tokyo's must-visit restaurants in the wagyu category.
en.reality: Upscale and fills up fast, and you can pay a great deal if you order the select cuts.
en.tip: Book through a hotel or a booking site, and choose a course served in small cuts.
en.baby_notes: An upscale, quiet place with small tables, not suitable for a stroller and a baby.
en.serves: High-end yakiniku, where you grill select cuts of wagyu yourselves on the grill. The dishes come in small portions, one after another.
en.kosher_note: You can order only beef and avoid pork dishes.
en.plan_line: Book ahead, fills up in the evenings
en.baby_block: Table grill smoke, not recommended for a baby

en.hype: In Gion, go with a guide, or you miss a lot.
en.reality: Busy in the evening, and there are rules, like no photographing geisha. A guide helps.
en.tip: Book an early afternoon tour, when you might see geisha on their way to appointments.
en.baby_notes: Fine with a stroller on the main streets, crowded in the narrow alleys in the evening.
en.todo: You walk with a guide through Gion and the wooden lanes of Hanamikoji. They explain geisha, tea houses and local customs.
en.special: You understand what you're looking at, not just taking photos. On the way you can stop at traditional tea houses and Yasaka Shrine.
en.plan_line: Book a guide ahead, walk 16:00–19:00

en.hype: Steps lined with red torii gates, like a small Fushimi Inari in central Tokyo.
en.reality: A quiet spot for photos, almost no crowds. The torii steps are shorter than the ones in Kyoto.
en.tip: Shoot the steps from the bottom for symmetry, then walk on to nearby Akasaka.
en.todo: Climb through the red torii gates to a quiet shrine in the Nagatacho area, and wander the grounds.
en.special: Like a pocket Fushimi Inari between office towers. At the entrance, monkeys guard the shrine instead of lions.
en.plan_line: Escalator at the east entrance, strollers can go up too

en.hype: A cheap neighborhood sushi place with high quality, and a good lunch deal on a nigiri set.
en.reality: Small and quiet. The lunch deal is popular, so come early.
en.tip: At lunch, get the nigiri set. It's good value.
en.baby_notes: Small sushi place with a counter, no room for a stroller.
en.serves: The chef makes nigiri (rice fingers topped with a slice of fish) in front of you, and lunch has a discounted set.
en.kosher_note: Order tuna, salmon, sea bream and yellowtail. Skip shrimp, octopus, squid, shellfish, sea urchin and eel.
en.plan_line: Better to book ahead, the area is busy after work
en.baby_block: Small place, may be smoky inside

en.hype: No menu. You tell the bartender which spirit or flavor you like, and he builds a custom drink.
en.reality: Ranked 14 in the 2022 Tabelog 100 (3.8), and about 4.5 on Google from around 842 ratings. The drinks are excellent, but a booking is hard to get and some complain about how seating works.
en.tip: Booking ahead only, through TableCheck. It opens around the 20th of the previous month and fills in minutes. Only 17 seats.
en.baby_notes: Not suitable for a baby: a small dim room with few seats and a late-night crowd.
en.serves: No menu. You tell the bartender which spirit or flavor you feel like and he mixes a drink on the spot. Behind the bar there are herbs, juniper branches and house infusions.
en.todo: The bar is on the 9th floor, usually open from 18:00. There's a cover charge, amount unknown.
en.special: Every drink is made from scratch to your taste, not off the shelf.
en.kosher_note: Cocktail bar without real food, so no pork or seafood problem.
en.plan_line: Small bar, booking required, closed Sundays
en.baby_block: Adults only bar, few seats, no stroller

en.hype: A little-known sushi place with high quality, mostly nigiri, and cheaper than similar spots.
en.reality: You have to book ahead, and the price is still high compared to everyday sushi.
en.tip: Book ahead and come hungry, most dishes are nigiri.
en.baby_notes: Small counter, no room for a stroller.
en.serves: Omakase sushi (chef's choice), mostly nigiri and a few small dishes.
en.kosher_note: Order tuna, salmon, sea bream and yellowtail. Skip shrimp, octopus, squid, shellfish, sea urchin and eel.
en.plan_line: Closed Mondays, book well ahead
en.baby_block: No stroller, 8 counter seats

en.hype: Ramen with a deep broth of dried sardines and unusual noodles, in a tiny shop at the top of a narrow staircase.
en.reality: The place is tiny and there's a queue at peak hours.
en.tip: Order the ramen with sardine broth. You can also come late at night.
en.baby_notes: Narrow stairs and a tiny space, you can't bring a stroller in.
en.serves: Ramen with dried sardine broth and special noodles. Strong flavor.
en.kosher_note: The broth is dried sardines, fine, but the dish comes with pork chashu, so ask for it without.
en.plan_line: Open 24 hours, only 10 seats, come off-peak
en.baby_block: Steep stairs to the 2nd floor, no stroller

en.hype: A Michelin-starred yakitori place, on Tokyo's must-eat lists.
en.reality: The set course also includes chicken organs.
en.tip: Book ahead, and if that's not for everyone, ask about a course without organs.
en.baby_notes: Small upscale place with a counter, no room for a stroller.
en.serves: Yakitori are chicken skewers grilled over charcoal. Here they serve different cuts, from breast to wings, with sauce or salt.
en.kosher_note: Most of the menu is chicken with no pork, but it's not a kosher-certified place, so ask about sides.
en.plan_line: Closed Sun and Mon, book up to 60 days ahead, evenings only
en.baby_block: Basement stairs, tight counter, hard with a stroller

en.hype: A Japanese whisky bar tucked in the lanes of Kagurazaka.
en.reality: Still fairly quiet, without lots of tourists.
en.tip: Book online through TableCheck and ask the staff which distillery they recommend.
en.serves: Most of the menu is Japanese whisky from independent distilleries, the kind you won't find in a regular shop. You drink it neat or in a cocktail, and there are small snacks too.
en.todo: A small, quiet bar open in the evening. Better to book a seat.
en.special: Specializes in small independent distilleries, not the big brands.
en.kosher_note: Whisky bar, no problem. If you order a snack, ask what's in it.
en.plan_line: Closed Sundays and holidays, better to book ahead
en.baby_block: Small whisky bar, not suitable for a baby

en.hype: On every list of Tokyo sights.
en.reality: The palace itself is closed to visitors, you only see the front and the moat. The East Gardens are nice, but many find it disappointing.
en.tip: Walk along the outer moat and skip the inner palace. Better to spend the time in Shinjuku Gyoen.
en.plan_line: East Gardens closed Mon, Fri and from 28 Dec; last entry 15:30

en.hype: Tempura at a chef's counter, a place people plan an evening around.
en.reality: Modest, comfortable atmosphere, and people praise the seafood and the chat with the chef. Ranked 94 in the 2025 Tabelog Tempura 100, score 3.6.
en.tip: The counter is small, so book ahead.
en.baby_notes: Adults' dinner at a counter, tight seating and no room for a stroller.
en.serves: The chef fries in front of you and serves each piece straight from the oil: seafood, shrimp and fish first, then seasonal vegetables in a thin batter. Rice or soup at the end.
en.todo: When you book, check the price and menu, because there's no set number.
en.special: A quiet, pleasant counter without heavy ceremony, and the chef really does talk with you.
en.kosher_note: There's also fish and vegetable tempura. Ask for no shrimp or seafood and make sure the oil is clean.
en.plan_line: Closed Sundays and the 3rd Saturday of the month (19 Dec)
en.baby_block: Tight counter, no stroller

en.hype: A ryokan especially good for babies, with in-room dining and more than 50 services for babies and kids.
en.reality: There's in-room dinner, a private open-air bath and baby services. Almost no guest reviews were found.
en.tip: You don't need special baby food, just milk. When you book, ask for hot water for bottles and a quiet spot to nurse.
en.baby_notes: In-room dinner for private feeding, a private bath, a free stroller loan and baby gear rental.
en.price: About ¥15,000–30,000 per person with two meals (varies)
en.todo: You get to Arima Onsen, a hot spring town in the mountains near Kobe, and stay at the ryokan. Book the private open-air bath, like Sakura, ahead and reserve an hour at check-in. There's a free shuttle from Arima Onsen station.
en.special: Arima is one of Japan's oldest hot spring areas, with brown-red, iron-rich water, and the bath and the meal here are private.
en.plan_line: Book the room meal ahead and ask for baby gear

en.hype: Small castella manju with a Hakone hot spring stamp, a classic snack where you watch the machine at work.
en.reality: Crisp outside, soft and moist inside. On the 2023 Tabelog 100 list.
en.tip: Buy a few hot to eat there, and a box to take home.
en.serves: Castella is a soft Japanese sponge cake, and here small fresh bites are baked in a machine, stamped with the Hakone hot spring mark. Usually a sweet filling inside, and you eat them warm from the bag.
en.todo: Buy a few at the stand at once, or a box of 10 or more. A light snack in Hakone-Yumoto, on the way from the station to the hot springs, and fine with a baby in a stroller.
en.special: You can stand and watch the machine bake, and it's a classic Hakone snack.
en.kosher_note: Sponge cake with a sweet filling, no pork and no seafood.
en.plan_line: Cash only, short queue before noon, around 10:00

en.hype: Classic Osaka okonomiyaki, on Tabelog's okonomiyaki lists.
en.reality: Tabelog score 3.24–3.32, average. Tasty and reasonably priced, but the decor is old and the sauce is sometimes sour.
en.tip: Good for a light meal, but if you only have one okonomiyaki, make it Ajinoya. The famous dish is the Deluxe Tama (squid, beef, shrimp).
en.plan_line: Almost no queue at weekday lunch, book for the evening

en.hype: A tea house in an impressive building with wooden beams, and on the second floor you get free pineapple cake and tea.
en.reality: Mostly a pineapple cake shop, and the free tasting is mainly meant for customers.
en.tip: Go up for the tasting on the second floor, and the building is worth a look from outside too.
en.baby_notes: The second floor is restricted, and it's not certain a stroller fits.
en.serves: A shop and tea house in a building with wooden beams designed by Kengo Kuma. You taste pineapple cake and tea.
en.kosher_note: Pineapple cake and tea, no pork and no seafood.
en.plan_line: Come before 18:00 for the free tasting

en.hype: Osaka's retro neon tower, lit up at night, with a famous slide from the observation deck.
en.reality: The night view and the neighborhood are the main thing. The deck is decent but smaller than expected.
en.tip: Come at sunset for the neon view.
en.price: About ¥900 for the deck, check before you go
en.todo: Walk around Shinsekai and take the elevator up the tower. At the top there's a view over Osaka, and on the way down you rub Billiken's foot for luck, or take the long slide. Afterwards eat kushikatsu (breaded fried skewers) or takoyaki (dough balls with octopus).
en.special: A nostalgic symbol of working-class Osaka, with neon signs and cheap restaurants all around, and best after dark.
en.plan_line: Be there by 18:30, last ascent 19:30, check hours first

en.hype: A shop from a trading house that has existed since 1716, selling Nara linen cloth and home goods.
en.reality: The flagship store in a historic building, where the brand started, with corners that tell the story of linen and its history.
en.tip: Open about 10:00–19:00. Year-end hours aren't published yet.
en.baby_notes: A fairly wide shop in Naramachi, and you can step out to a quiet street with the stroller.
en.todo: Look at towels, napkins and cloth made from Nara linen, and Japanese-design household and kitchen items. Then stroll the nearby Naramachi streets.
en.special: Japanese design you actually use at home, not another souvenir, and the cloth is a Nara tradition.
en.plan_line: Open daily, check hours on the website first

en.hype: A quiet green island a few minutes from Shinjuku station, with wide paths and lawns.
en.reality: 4.6 on Google from about 39,800 reviews. People praise the greenhouse and the Japanese gardens. Busy at midday and in cherry blossom season, and autumn was less impressive than expected.
en.tip: From the New South exit of Shinjuku station there's a route with an elevator. The grounds have plenty of nursing rooms and changing stations.
en.baby_notes: Wide paths and open lawns suit a stroller, but the nursing rooms have no hot water.
en.price: Small entrance fee for adults, children under 6 free. Check the price on the website.
en.todo: Enter through the gate and walk wide, flat paths between huge lawns. There are three styles: a Japanese garden with ponds and bridges, a French garden with an avenue of trees, and an English garden with lots of lawn. You can also go into the tropical greenhouse and the traditional tea room.
en.special: A quiet green island in one of the most crowded areas in the world. Alcohol isn't allowed, so the mood is calm and good for families.
en.plan_line: Come on a weekday morning, last entry in winter 16:00

en.hype: An Edo-themed sento with yukata and street food, popular on social media.
en.reality: Both locals and tourists come, and it's one of Tokyo's well-known public baths.
en.tip: Come in the evening, rent a yukata and eat before you go in. Tattoo rules vary, so check ahead.
en.plan_line: Closed in 2021. Replacement: Manyo Club Toyosu, open 24/7
en.baby_block: Diapered babies likely not allowed in the baths

en.hype: Wonderful sushi, a friendly atmosphere, good value for the price, and easy to book.
en.reality: Fairly expensive, and you need to book ahead.
en.tip: Book ahead and mention any food restrictions.
en.baby_notes: High-end sushi place with a counter only, no room for a stroller.
en.serves: High-level omakase sushi at the counter, in a friendly atmosphere.
en.kosher_note: Ask for no shrimp, octopus, squid, shellfish, sea urchin or eel, and eat tuna, salmon and sea bream.
en.plan_line: Closed Sundays, omakase at fixed seatings, book ahead
en.baby_block: Quiet counter, no stroller

en.hype: Feed the deer and film them bowing for a cracker, the most talked-about Nara clip online.
en.reality: Very crowded near the entrance, and the deer get pushy when you hold crackers.
en.tip: Walk ten minutes past the crowd at the entrance, toward Mount Wakakusa, where the deer are calmer. If you only want a photo, skip the busy main path.
en.plan_line: Take crackers out only when ready to feed, the deer push and butt

en.hype: Okonomiyaki with a Michelin Bib Gourmand, famous for its yamaimo batter (grated mountain yam) and long queues online.
en.reality: The queues are real, but most visitors say it's worth it. Tabelog score 3.57 from about 1,600 reviews.
en.tip: 5 minutes' walk from Namba station, exit 14. Come at opening or at a quiet hour, and the signature is the yamaimo version.
en.serves: Okonomiyaki is a griddled cabbage pancake. Here the batter uses yamaimo instead of flour, so it's soft and airy. Topped with sauce, mayo and fish flakes.
en.todo: On weekend evenings the queue is 30–90 minutes, so lunch is better. A dish costs about ¥1,400–2,800. Open 11:00–22:00, and the closing day is unclear (probably Thursday), so check first.
en.special: The yamaimo batter is the reason to come here in particular.
en.kosher_note: Order the yamaimo-yaki or a beef version, no pork, seafood or bacon. The fish flakes on top are fine.
en.plan_line: Long queue, no bookings, come at opening or before 17:00

en.hype: Anime and collector heaven, the main Mandarake store.
en.reality: The layout is confusing and some shops are closed or run down, but the staff are nice and prices are lower than Akihabara.
en.tip: Most hobby shops are on the upper floors. Check the floor maps and come on a weekday.
en.todo: Enter through the Nakano Sun Mall arcade into a closed, maze-like complex, and wander the upper floors among dozens of anime, manga and collectibles shops, mostly Mandarake. The basement has food stalls and ice cream for a break.
en.special: Small, focused collector shops, with a less touristy feel. Easy to lose a few hours there.
en.plan_line: Most shops open after noon, don't come in the morning
en.baby_block: Crowded, stairs, hard with a stroller, use a carrier

en.hype: One of Tokyo's must-try coffee places.
en.reality: A small, crowded spot with no seating, so you drink standing or take it away.
en.tip: Tell the barista what flavor you like and he picks suitable beans.
en.baby_notes: No seating and no room for a stroller, only good for a quick coffee.
en.serves: Specialty coffee, beans from several roasters chosen to match your taste. You can get filter, espresso or a milk drink.
en.kosher_note: Coffee and milk drinks are fine, but it's not a kosher-certified place.
en.plan_line: Quietest at opening, 10:00
en.baby_block: No stroller, almost no seating

en.hype: A Scandinavian-style cafe, popular on Instagram, and a cocktail bar in the evening.
en.reality: Good Google ratings, but the coffee isn't impressive and the place is always full of people taking photos.
en.tip: On a weekday morning it's easier to find a seat. In the evening you come for the atmosphere and the cocktails.
en.plan_line: Tiny place, with a stroller sit outside on the bench

en.hype: A wooden baby room, quiet and lovely, built for ages 0–2.
en.reality: The baby room is calm, with wooden pull toys and shape sorters, a nursing corner and a changing room. The staff are nice, and the entrance fee is a bit high.
en.tip: Buy a ticket online for a one-hour entry slot in the baby room. Children aged 3 and up, siblings too, can't enter. Check hours on the website.
en.baby_notes: Meant for up to about age 2, with a nursing corner and a changing room in the baby area.
en.price: Adults about ¥800–1,100 online, children cheaper, under 6 months free
en.todo: The museum is in a former primary school building near Yotsuya-sanchome (Marunouchi line, exit 2, 5–7 minutes' walk). You get a ticket for one hour and go straight to the wooden baby room, a soft, quiet room where the baby crawls and tries safe wooden toys, and you sit with them on the floor.
