en.special: Everything is natural wood, with no screens and no flashing plastic, and the guides are volunteers who play with the children.
en.plan_line: Open 10:00–16:00, closed Thursdays, ticket ahead for entry slot

en.hype: An obanzai set with delicate seasonal dishes, Kyoto the way you see it on Instagram.
en.reality: A pleasant seasonal atmosphere, but people who show up without a booking are usually turned away.
en.tip: Come at lunch, when the seasonal set is the most reliable.
en.serves: Obanzai is Kyoto home cooking. The set comes as several small plates of simmered vegetables, fish and tofu, depending on the season. Everything is delicate and light.
en.todo: Order one set, you don't build your own. Check the exact price when you book, and you might be able to ask for a baby-friendly spot.
en.special: Obanzai in a modern design that looks great in photos, in the Nishiki area, Kyoto's famous market district.
en.kosher_note: Some plates include shrimp or seafood, so ask for it without.
en.plan_line: Two seatings only, 11:30–15:00, book online

en.hype: The heart of Osaka's youth and vintage culture.
en.reality: A dense grid of small streets, about 350 meters, with lots of secondhand shops and record shops in basements. Worth it if you like rummaging, less if you're looking for something specific.
en.tip: Carry on to nearby Orange Street (Tachibana-dori) for more upscale vintage.
en.baby_notes: Narrow alleys and crowded sidewalks, awkward with a stroller.
en.todo: Stroll among the vintage and clothing shops and go down into the basements of the record shops. Good for jackets, jeans and Japanese items you can't find at home.
en.special: Right next to the Shinsaibashi arcade, so you can combine both in one walk.
en.plan_line: Hours vary, from about 11:00, better in the afternoon

en.hype: Vegan and vegetarian ramen, and some call it the best ramen they've had.
en.reality: The place is small, and there may be a queue at mealtimes.
en.tip: Come before the lunch crush and order the vegan bowl.
en.baby_notes: Small place, not much room for a stroller.
en.serves: Vegan and vegetarian ramen in Kyoto, with a plant-based broth and noodles.
en.kosher_note: Order the vegan or vegetarian bowls, no pork or seafood. It's not a kosher-certified place.
en.plan_line: Book a table ahead on TableCheck

en.hype: Conveyor-belt sushi that you order from a screen, good fish and huge portions, fine even if you're new to sushi.
en.reality: The pieces are big and it's easy to order too much. At peak hours you wait for a table.
en.tip: Order a few pieces at a time from the screen, so the fish arrives fresh.
en.baby_notes: Counter seats and small booths, no comfortable room for a stroller.
en.serves: Conveyor-belt sushi turned into screen ordering, with extra-large nigiri and thick cuts of fish.
en.kosher_note: Tick only tuna, salmon, sea bream and yellowtail on the screen, and skip shrimp, octopus, squid, shellfish and eel.
en.plan_line: No bookings, arrive before 11:30 or after 14:00

en.hype: A retro underground cafe with a mysterious atmosphere.
en.reality: Tabelog score about 3.7, quiet and not yet full of tourists.
en.tip: Good for a quiet afternoon coffee. It's in the basement (B1F), so look for the sign.
en.serves: A kissaten, an old-style Japanese coffee house, in a basement. Hand-made coffee, strong and bitter, and you can add toast or cake. The place is known for its cold cheesecake. Dark, retro mood.
en.todo: No bookings, just walk in. Cash only, about ¥1,000 per person. Smoking is allowed, which is less pleasant for a baby.
en.special: Chosen for the Tabelog Kissaten 100 in 2021 and 2022.
en.kosher_note: Coffee, toast or cake. Make sure the toast has no ham.
en.plan_line: Closed on weekends, check hours and address
en.baby_block: Basement, probably stairs only

en.hype: Yudofu (simmered tofu) in a temple garden, in every Kyoto food reel.
en.reality: Creative tofu courses, a garden view and staff who look after vegans. Some found it pricey for what you get.
en.tip: Come at lunch rather than in the evening, when it's less busy. Through Klook it works out much more expensive.
en.serves: Yudofu: cubes of tofu simmered in a small pot of water and kelp, eaten hot with a dipping sauce. The course adds other tofu dishes, like fried tofu and vegetables. Gentle, warming food, good for December.
en.todo: Book on TableCheck for groups of 2 to 4, and by phone for bigger groups (075-761-2311). Lunch courses cost ¥8,200, ¥10,700 or ¥13,400 per person.
en.special: You eat in a house by Nanzenji temple, with a Japanese garden, and the tofu comes in all kinds of variations.
en.kosher_note: Tofu and vegetables only, so it works. The broth sometimes has bonito, which is fine for you.
en.plan_line: Book directly with the restaurant, closed for year-end break

en.hype: A pleasant bakery and cafe in Daikanyama, with a terrace.
en.reality: Tabelog score 3.63 from about 1,000 reviews. A solid place, nothing out of the ordinary.
en.tip: Call ahead and check stroller access.
en.baby_notes: Children are welcome and the terrace (80 of the 96 seats) may suit a stroller, but the stroller route and nursing weren't checked.
en.serves: More than 50 kinds of pastry a day. The star is the shio-butter melon pan: brioche dough with a crisp crust and salted butter melting inside. There's also a plate of breads with soup and a drink, and avocado toast with coffee.
en.todo: Opens at 8:30, so it's best to come early when everything is fresh and not sold out. Eat the roll within about an hour, while the butter is still soft. A bread plate with soup and a drink is about ¥1,800, check the current price.
en.special: The salted butter roll is the reason to come, and only a limited number are sold each day.
en.kosher_note: Most pastries are sweet or buttery. With the savory breads, check there's no bacon or ham.
en.plan_line: Long weekend queue at noon, come early, sit on the terrace

en.hype: A six-seat sushi counter that guides recommend for special occasions.
en.reality: Has won a Tabelog Bronze award every year since 2018, with a score of 4.29. You book about two months ahead.
en.tip: Booking only through the Tabelog listing. Confirm hours and holiday dates by phone, because the restaurant moved and changed its name.
en.baby_notes: Omakase at a six-seat counter for adults, not suitable for a baby.
en.serves: Six chairs at a counter, and one chef makes sushi in front of you, piece by piece. No menu, it's omakase: fresh fish by season, each cut on a small ball of rice, and you eat each bite straight from his hand.
en.todo: There's no menu, you just sit and eat. Check with them ahead about bringing a baby.
en.special: Sushi for a special occasion, at a counter for only six people.
en.kosher_note: The course usually has shrimp, shellfish and caviar, so when you book ask for fish with fins and scales only.
en.plan_line: Only 6 seats, booking required
en.baby_block: 6 bar seats, not suitable for a baby

en.hype: A viral mochi shop: the staff pound the dough in front of you, and kinako is sprinkled by hand on the yomogi mochi.
en.reality: Tabelog score 3.72–3.73, and on Tabelog's 2023 Dessert 100 list. Crowded during the mochi-pounding demos, so come early.
en.tip: Get the yomogi mochi with red bean and the warabi mochi, and come early to skip the queue.
en.serves: A mochi shop where the dough is pounded right in front of you. The famous item is yomogi mochi, green mochi with Japanese mugwort and anko filling (sweet red bean paste), with kinako sprinkled on top, a powder of roasted soy flour. Soft and very fresh.
en.todo: Buy and eat standing near the shop. The demo has no fixed time, about every half hour when there's a crowd, and ends around 15:00.
en.special: Won the speed mochi-pounding championship in 2005 and 2006, and a demo like that happens a few times a day.
en.kosher_note: Mochi with sweet bean and soy flour, no pork and no seafood.
en.plan_line: Queue moves fast, check Instagram to see if it's closed

en.hype: Kyoto's kitchen: a covered market five blocks long with tako tamago, tamagoyaki, grilled eel and yatsuhashi.
en.reality: Crowded, and some stalls are priced for tourists. The main stalls (tako tamago, tamagoyaki with dashi, pickles) are worth it, and tasting samples is common.
en.tip: Come between 10 and 11, before the crowds, try the samples and skip the places with seating, which cost a lot more.
en.serves: A long covered market where you eat standing as you walk: tako tamago (a small octopus stuffed with a quail egg on a skewer), tamagoyaki (sweet Japanese omelet with dashi broth), pickles and desserts.
en.todo: No booking, just walk in. Many stalls don't let you eat while walking, so you stand by the stall. Bring cash.
en.special: The "kitchen of Kyoto", five blocks of stalls. The really good ones justify the bustle.
en.kosher_note: Tamagoyaki, pickles and desserts are fine. Skip the tako tamago (octopus) and the seafood skewers.
en.plan_line: Come in the morning before the crush, many stalls close at 17:00
en.baby_block: Crowded alley, hard with a stroller, carrier better

en.hype: Thick canvas bags from a family workshop in Kyoto that has been running since 1905.
en.reality: Bags of cotton and thick canvas, hand sewn, that started as work sacks for carpenters and milk sellers. The design is simple and doesn't try to impress tourists.
en.tip: Come early in the morning, the popular models sell out. Hours and stock are unclear, so check the website.
en.baby_notes: Strong shoulder and back bags, which also work as a diaper bag.
en.todo: Try a few bags on your shoulder and check the pockets and seams. You can buy a backpack or a simple tote, or a hat.
en.special: A local brand with no physical store anywhere else in the world, and they'll repair a torn bag for you.
en.plan_line: Closed Tuesdays and at year-end

en.hype: Clear ramen with a deep, flavorful broth, one of the best around.
en.reality: The queue can take a few hours.
en.tip: Come early and order the clear ramen.
en.baby_notes: Long queue and a small space, not suitable for a stroller.
en.serves: Chinese-style clear ramen with a deep broth and thin noodles.
en.kosher_note: The broth is based on fish and pork, so better to skip it.
en.plan_line: Get there before 11:30, there's a queue
en.baby_block: Small counter, queue outside, no stroller

en.hype: Juicy wagyu inside crisp rice buns, like a burger but completely different.
en.reality: Street food in a tourist area, so there's a queue and the price is fairly high.
en.tip: Eat on the spot right away, while the bun is still crisp.
en.baby_notes: Street food you take in your hand, easy with a stroller.
en.serves: Juicy wagyu beef inside crisp rice buns, burger style.
en.kosher_note: Beef, no pork or seafood. Ask about the sauce.
en.plan_line: No Tabelog booking, call ahead and confirm hours

en.hype: A big, old tea house full of charm, where you take off your shoes and sit on tatami.
en.reality: Far from the city center, and there's a ¥100 entrance fee.
en.tip: Take off your shoes and sit by the garden with tea and a sweet.
en.baby_notes: A big, quiet house. Leave the stroller at the entrance and sit on the tatami with the baby. Good for nursing too.
en.serves: An old Japanese house with a garden. You sit on tatami, drink tea and eat a Japanese sweet.
en.kosher_note: Japanese tea and sweets, no pork and no seafood.
en.plan_line: Open until 17:00, last entry 16:30, better in the morning

en.hype: A small six-seat bar that Kyoto food people pass along, by personal booking only.
en.reality: Tabelog 4.35 and Google 4.6 from only 21 reviews.
en.tip: Six seats and one dinner service a night. Ask about the seating when you book.
en.baby_notes: A six-seat bar with one seating a night, no known baby facilities or stroller access.
en.serves: A seasonal Japanese meal at a six-seat counter. Small dishes come one after another, based on what's in season that week. In December usually winter fish and hot stews, and the menu changes.
en.todo: You can't just walk in, you book through a hotel or someone who knows the place. Check how to book before you lock in plans. A long meal at a small counter, not comfortable with a baby.
en.special: Only six chairs, and a Tabelog Silver award for 2026. It's not clear if it's kaiseki (a formal course) or a meal at the counter.
en.kosher_note: A fixed meal the chef decides, usually with a lot of seafood. Ask when booking for no pork or seafood, but they may not be able to adjust.
en.plan_line: Book well ahead through a hotel, address not published
en.baby_block: Six counter seats, not suitable for a baby

en.hype: A modern tea house in Tokyo, and you should take the full course.
en.reality: The price is high for tea.
en.tip: Order the full course, and book ahead in busy periods.
en.baby_notes: A quiet, delicate place with counter seating, not suitable for a stroller.
en.serves: A modern tea house serving a tasting course of Japanese tea alongside a delicate Japanese sweet.
en.kosher_note: Japanese tea and sweets, no pork or seafood.
en.plan_line: Small tea bar, booking required, cancellation fee
en.baby_block: Small quiet bar, about 10 seats, hard with a stroller

en.hype: A covered street with vintage boutiques from the 60s to the 90s, loved by secondhand fans in Tokyo.
en.reality: Less crowded than Shimokitazawa, with friendly sellers and real finds. Prices run from cheap to expensive.
en.tip: Set aside half a day for both sides of the station. Treasure Factory Style is the place for upscale secondhand.
en.todo: Enter the covered street by Koenji station, which splits into several lanes, and wander among vintage, secondhand, record and small boutique shops. Stop to eat at an izakaya (Japanese pub with food) or a small cafe, and go over to the other side of the station too.
en.special: A neighborhood of alternative culture, not a mall, and the covered roof helps in cold and rain.
en.plan_line: Most shops open after 11:00, better in the afternoon

en.hype: A ryokan in Hakone that takes babies, with in-room dining and several private baths.
en.reality: Rated 4.1 on Jalan from 806 reviews. Good for a three-generation trip with a baby, with in-room dining and two kinds of private bath.
en.tip: Book through Jalan, Rakuten or the official site, and confirm baby gear ahead (bouncer, bottle warmer), because stock is limited.
en.baby_notes: In-room meals, free private bath and baby gear loan (limited stock). Check ahead that the baby can go in the private bath.
en.price: About ¥25,000–40,000 per person with two meals (varies by package and season)
en.todo: Take a short train ride from Hakone-Yumoto to Tonosawa station and stay at the ryokan, sleeping on tatami and eating dinner and breakfast in your room. There's a free private indoor bath, and a paid outdoor bath (Kanzan no Yu) across a suspension bridge. In between, relax in a yukata, a light cotton robe.
en.special: A real ryokan with an overnight stay, onsen and in-room meals, in private baths. Tonosawa is much quieter than touristy Hakone.
en.plan_line: Book the private bath by phone ahead, 50 minutes
en.baby_block: Hanging bridge to the outdoor bath, no stroller

en.hype: A Kyoto-style kaiseki restaurant that welcomes families and arranges a private room for babies.
en.reality: Tabelog score 3.9–4.15 from about 480 reviews, and Tripadvisor 4.2 from 83. Families praise the kids' menu.
en.tip: Book a private room ahead and call to confirm the baby can join. Ask for the kids' menu.
en.baby_notes: Strollers are accepted and there's a private room for babies. Young children are only allowed in private rooms.
en.serves: Kaiseki in Kyoto: a traditional Japanese meal of several small, beautifully arranged dishes. Lunch has three courses, at ¥13,000, ¥25,000 and ¥35,000, plus a special kids' course.
en.todo: Lunch only on Mondays, Fridays, Saturdays and Sundays. With a baby, ask for a private room, because at the counter only children from age 12 are allowed. There's a ¥3,000 room charge, and it's unclear if that applies at lunch, so ask by phone: 075-223-3200.
en.special: A branch of the Wakuden group, a known name in Kyoto, that welcomes families warmly and offers a private room so it's relaxed with children.
en.kosher_note: Fixed courses with seafood. Ask when booking for no pork or seafood. There's also a simpler kids' course.
en.plan_line: Book about a month ahead, closed Wed and year-end holidays
en.baby_block: No children at the counter, private room only

en.hype: The Pontocho branch of STAR BAR from Ginza, a classic cocktail bar with a low counter.
en.reality: Tabelog 3.68 from about 138 reviews. Pontocho is touristy, so this isn't a local secret.
en.tip: On the fifth lane of Pontocho, about 244 meters from Sanjo station. Check booking on Tabelog.
en.baby_notes: A small counter-style cocktail bar in an alley, adults only and not suitable for a 5-month-old.
en.serves: A small cocktail bar with a low counter, in the classic Japanese bar style where the bartender makes every drink by hand. You can have a cocktail or Japanese whisky, and for dessert kakigori, finely shaved ice with syrup.
en.todo: Pontocho is touristy in the evening, so come early. It's not known if you need to book, so worth asking ahead. An evening bar with a narrow counter, so maybe take turns going.
en.special: A branch of the famous STAR BAR from Ginza. Chosen for Tabelog's Bar 100 in 2022, rank 36, and it's unclear if it's still on the list.
en.kosher_note: Cocktails, whisky and sweet shaved ice, no pork and no seafood.
en.plan_line: Opens in the afternoon, hours unverified, check Google Maps
en.baby_block: Evening bar, not suitable for a baby

en.hype: Excellent tempura, and the set with a tempura egg on a rice bowl is the one to get.
en.reality: Sometimes the queue is long, but it moves fast.
en.tip: Order the tempura set with the egg on rice, and come before peak hours.
en.baby_notes: Small place with few seats and the queue outside, no room for a stroller.
en.serves: Tempura is vegetables and seafood in a light batter, fried crisp. Here it's served on a rice bowl with a tempura egg, shrimp, pumpkin and more.
en.kosher_note: There's shrimp and fish too. Ask for it without and stay with vegetables and egg.
en.plan_line: Queue starts before the lunch opening, closed Mondays
en.baby_block: Tiny restaurant, queue outside, hard with a stroller

en.hype: A hidden standing bar (tachinomi) in Fukushima, with creative small dishes and a deep sake list.
en.reality: Tabelog score 3.58 from 267 reviews, about 5 minutes from Fukushima station.
en.tip: Standing is fine but not required. Come early or midweek, because small bars like this fill up fast.
en.baby_notes: A small standing bar, not suitable for a baby. Save it for an adults' evening.
en.serves: A small standing bar in Fukushima, Osaka. Sake by the glass from a long list, with small creative seasonal dishes the chef makes on the spot. You eat standing and move on to another glass.
en.todo: Walk in, order a glass and two small dishes, and move on. It's an evening bar, less suitable with a baby.
en.special: Chosen for Tabelog's Standing Bar Hyakumeiten 2025, the 100 best standing bars in Japan, and still quiet and free of tourists.
en.kosher_note: Sake bar with changing small dishes. Ask the chef and order only what has no pork or seafood.
en.plan_line: Book online, only about 10 spots at the standing bar
en.baby_block: Narrow standing bar, no stroller room

en.hype: A lesser-known seafood market that food fans find off the tourist trail.
en.reality: Prices are lower than Kuromon and the crowd is mostly local buyers. There are few reviews, so check before you go.
en.tip: Opens early, about 4:00–11:00, on Mon, Tue and Thu–Sat. The sushi near the entrance is a good first stop.
en.serves: A local fish market where you buy fresh fish and seafood. Think sashimi, uni (sea urchin gonads, creamy and sweet) and shellfish, tasting of the sea with little processing.
en.todo: Worth coming in the morning, and bring cash.
en.special: Far fewer tourists, so it feels like the real Osaka.
en.kosher_note: There's fin-fish sashimi like salmon and tuna, but most of the place is uni, shellfish and other seafood, so be picky.
en.plan_line: Wholesale market, come by 9:00, closed Sundays and holidays
en.baby_block: Wholesale market, trucks, wet floor, hard with a stroller

en.hype: A hidden matcha roastery in Uji, with an inner garden and matcha-yuzu gelato that looks great on Instagram.
en.reality: People praise the design, the charging outlets and the option to choose your matcha strength.
en.tip: Combine it with a walk along the river in Uji and the shops near Byodo-in.
en.baby_notes: Unknown if there are stairs or room for a stroller, check before you go.
en.serves: A roastery and cafe in Uji, where Japan's most famous matcha grows. They roast the leaves and make matcha, and you choose how strong. There's also matcha-yuzu ice cream and a matcha latte.
en.todo: Just walk in. Uji is 30–40 minutes from Kyoto by train.
en.special: A hidden spot with a quiet inner garden, away from the crowds of central Kyoto.
en.kosher_note: Matcha, ice cream and latte, all fine.
en.plan_line: No bookings, go in the morning, call to check 28–31 Dec hours

en.hype: A viral tonkotsu ramen chain with single-person booths and long tourist queues.
en.reality: Good but not exceptional, and the queue is mostly hype. Some say it's worth the wait, which can reach about two hours.
en.tip: Fine for once, but better to skip the queue and go to a neighborhood ramen shop, which is better value.
en.plan_line: Open 24/7, almost no queue early or late
en.baby_block: Basement down stairs, hard with a stroller, fold it

en.hype: Tokyo's vintage capital, with dozens of shops in small lanes.
en.reality: There's variety: chains like Chicago and Flamingo are cheaper, while independent shops like Jarmusch and Link Ray are more curated and pricier. The neighborhood is nice even without shopping, with cafes and small theaters.
en.tip: Come in the afternoon, but not too late, because it gets dark early. Small shops don't always take cards, so bring cash.
en.baby_notes: Narrow lanes and small shops, not comfortable with a stroller. Better to come without the baby.
en.todo: Leave the station and wander among the shops, trying on and comparing prices. Stop for a coffee or curry in between, and ask the sellers to show you what just came in.
en.special: Dozens of secondhand shops in one neighborhood is rare, including American clothes from the 80s and 90s.
en.plan_line: Most shops open at 12:00, better in the afternoon

en.hype: A classic public bath in Arima, with rust-brown, iron-rich kinsen water, loved by day-trippers from Kansai for years.
en.reality: Reopened on 17 March 2026 after renovation, open 8:00–22:00. Popular and busy, more classic than hidden.
en.tip: Come on weekdays or late evening, before the rush. There are rules about tattoos and towels, so bring a towel or buy one there.
en.baby_notes: The bath is split by gender, so it suits an adults' evening while the other couple stays with the baby.
en.price: About ¥650 on weekdays, ¥800 on weekends. A combo ticket with Gin no Yu is about ¥1,200, check the current price.
en.todo: Travel about an hour from Osaka-Umeda, by bus or by train via Shin-Kobe, to the hot spring town of Arima and go into the public bath. Bathing is separate for men and women, in a hot pool of reddish-brown water. Then stroll the town's lanes, and you can add Gin no Yu with its clear water.
en.special: The reddish water, rich in iron and salt, is Arima's trademark, one of Japan's oldest hot spring towns, and in December a hot soak after the cold is the point.
en.plan_line: Closed 2nd and 4th Tuesdays, check before going at year-end
en.baby_block: Gender-split baths, stairs, baby likely not allowed

en.hype: A first-night package for babies aged 0–2, at a ryokan in Arima with gold-water (kinsen, 金泉) baths.
en.reality: No reviews. The package listing is valid until 31 October 2026, so you need to confirm it again for your dates.
en.tip: Ask the ryokan directly if the 0–2 first-night package is available on your dates. The kinsen water, golden and iron-rich, can be strong, so check whether a 5-month-old can bathe in it.
en.baby_notes: In-room meal, a private outdoor bath (by booking, not in every room), a baby bath and unlimited diapers.
en.price: About ¥20,000–35,000 per person with two meals (varies)
en.todo: Go for a day or two to Arima, a hot spring town near Kobe, and stay at the ryokan (traditional Japanese inn) on the 0–2 baby package. Meals come to your room, and there's a private outdoor bath and a small baby bath. Everything is slow, no rushing between sights.
en.special: Arima is famous for kinsen water, reddish-brown and rich in iron, and is one of Japan's oldest hot spring towns. The package is built for babies, which is rare in Japan.
en.plan_line: Ask ahead about day entry and a private bath for the baby

en.hype: Kyoto's historic tea shop, with more than 150 years of tea from Uji.
en.reality: A real shop, not a tourist trap, with a wide range of sencha, hojicha and matcha at every price level. Open 10:00–17:00, and the Kaboku Tearoom in the courtyard is mostly for sitting, not shopping.
en.tip: Check the year-end hours on the website: last year the tea room was closed 29–31 December and the whole shop 1–3 January.
en.baby_notes: The shop is small but comfortable with a stroller at quiet hours, and you don't need to sit in the tea room to buy.
en.todo: Walk in, ask for a taste, and ask the staff which tea suits a gift and which suits home. Buy a few sealed tea bags and maybe matcha for everyday. If the baby is calm, you can sit in the tea room for a cup of matcha.
en.special: High-level Japanese tea without the tourist queue of the chain shops, and the tea bags are packed nicely as gifts.
en.plan_line: Closed 2nd Wed of the month, tea room limited in late Dec

en.hype: The world-famous crossing that every TikTok Japan reel opens with.
en.reality: A quick photo and you're out. Don't come at peak hours, and there's no reason to plan a whole evening around it.
en.tip: Film from inside the Starbucks or from the Shibuya Sky viewing deck, instead of fighting the crowd at the crossing.
en.plan_line: Watch for free from the Mark City bridge, then cross yourselves

en.hype: The most famous food hall in Tokyo's department stores, with bento stalls, sweets and sushi.
en.reality: About 180 stalls in a large basement. Crowded at peak hours, but the quality is consistent.
en.tip: Come on a weekday morning. Get bento or sweets to go, and it's worth a look at the sushi counters.
en.todo: Go down to the basement floors of Isetan in Shinjuku and wander among stalls of bento, sushi, pastries, Japanese and French desserts, fruit and tea. Taste what's offered and buy ready food to take to the hotel or a picnic, or boxed sweets as gifts. People usually don't sit and eat there, you take it with you.
en.special: The food is displayed like jewelry, and it's an easy way to eat lots of real Japanese dishes without booking a restaurant.
en.plan_line: Weekday mornings, before the crowds. 31 Dec open until 17:00

en.hype: An atmospheric lantern lane in the evening, the most photographed street in Kyoto on Instagram and TikTok.
en.reality: Some call it a tourist trap. The food on the main street is pricey and weaker than a few streets away, but the evening atmosphere is real.
en.tip: Walk through at dusk for the photos, and eat a few streets away, where it's cheaper and better. Don't book at the tourist restaurants on the main street.
en.plan_line: Most places in the lane are small, book ahead or come before 18:00

en.hype: A Fuji view framed by flowers, and the shot with the Lawson and Fuji is among the most famous at the Fuji Five Lakes.
en.reality: Kawaguchiko is the most touristy lake, and sometimes Fuji is hidden in clouds, so the view can disappoint.
en.tip: Skip it if the forecast is cloudy. Lake Shoji has quieter views of Fuji.
en.plan_line: Fuji looks best in the morning, in the afternoon it's usually in cloud

en.hype: A three-Michelin-star sushi restaurant that food fans compare to Sushi Saito.
en.reality: Tabelog 4.35, and counted among the best sushi in Tokyo. Some find the rice too salty for the price.
en.tip: Hard to get a seat, so book well ahead through the Tabelog listing or a concierge. Confirm the address, because it's unclear if it's Ginza or Azabu-Juban.
en.baby_notes: A Michelin-level omakase bar for adults, not suitable for a baby.
en.price: Premium omakase, about ¥50,000–80,000 per person without drinks (worth confirming)
en.serves: Omakase at the counter: you sit facing the chef and he places nigiri (a piece of fish on rice) in front of you one after another, straight from his hand. The fish is seasonal and the chef chooses for you. The rice is Edomae style, seasoned with red vinegar, and the toro (fatty tuna belly) melts in the mouth.
en.todo: Open in the evenings only. With a 5-month-old at a quiet counter like this it's not simple, so check ahead.
en.special: A small counter, and people who know say it's one of the best places in Tokyo.
en.kosher_note: Omakase the chef picks, usually with shrimp, shellfish and caviar. Ask when booking for fin fish only like tuna and salmon, though they may not agree.
en.plan_line: Sushi bar, booking only, closed Sundays and holidays
en.baby_block: Quiet sushi bar, not suitable for a baby

en.hype: Yuzu shio ramen with a glowing golden broth, very popular on Instagram.
en.reality: A light, refreshing broth with a gentle touch of yuzu. A refined bowl, not an explosion of strong flavor.
en.tip: Order the yuzu shio ramen. Open until about 5 in the morning, so it suits after a bar.
en.serves: Ramen in a clear, light broth with yuzu (a Japanese citrus) and a salt base, with slices of chashu (seasoned roast pork) and toppings. The taste is fresh and delicate, and you can ask for a richer broth.
en.todo: Buy a ticket at the machine by the entrance and hand it to the staff at the bar. A bowl costs about ¥1,100–1,800, check at the machine.
en.special: The yuzu broth is the signature, and its golden color makes noise on Instagram.
en.kosher_note: The broth is light and not pork-based, but it comes with pork chashu, so ask for no chashu or the vegan version.
en.plan_line: Card or mobile payment only, no cash; check year-end hours

en.hype: A marutto matcha parfait served in a bamboo tube, an Uji dessert people post online.
en.reality: On Tabelog's 2023 Dessert Cafes 100 list, for the West area.
en.tip: Get the marutto parfait and the nama matcha jelly, and at lunch you can try the soba tea noodles. Open about 10:00–19:00, check before you go.
en.serves: A matcha cafe in Uji. The famous dessert is the marutto parfait, matcha in a bamboo cup with ice cream, jelly, azuki (sweet beans) and cake crumbs. There's also nama matcha jelly, soft and cold, and hot matcha.
en.todo: No bookings, you take a number at the entrance and wait. On weekends the wait is an hour or more. A parfait is about ¥1,200–2,200, and meanwhile you can walk to Uji Bridge.
en.special: The long-established tea house of Uji, and its main branch.
en.kosher_note: Matcha and tea desserts, all sweet, no pork or seafood.
en.plan_line: Arrive before the 10:00 opening, the queue can be long

en.hype: A small, friendly cafe.
en.reality: Small, and hard to find a seat at busy times.
en.tip: Go to the upper floor and try to get a spot by the window.
en.baby_notes: Small place with stairs and little room for a stroller.
en.serves: A local cafe in Nakameguro with quality coffee and other drinks.
en.kosher_note: Coffee and drinks, no pork or seafood.
en.plan_line: Come in the morning before the weekend queue

en.hype: Yakitori from Tajima chicken, the casual sister of the high-end restaurant Goichi.
en.reality: Tabelog score 3.62 from about 468 reviews.
en.tip: Cash only, 30 seats, near Tenma station. Better to book, and there's also an all-you-can-eat-and-drink course up to ¥8,000.
en.baby_notes: Adults-only evening, a lively yakitori counter focused on alcohol, not set up for a baby.
en.serves: Yakitori, chicken skewers over charcoal, from quality Tajima chicken. You get small juicy skewers one after another, including tsukune (chicken meatball on a skewer). Some courses also include chicken sukiyaki.
en.todo: Book through the online form, and for courses you usually pay in advance. A yakitori course is about ¥4,800 per person, and pricier courses are ¥7,000–8,000. Open in the evening from 17:00, and on weekends at lunch too. Prices differ between sites, so confirm.
en.special: Chosen for the Tabelog Yakitori 100 West three years in a row, an izakaya mood without the formality.
en.kosher_note: Charcoal chicken yakitori. Make sure there are no pork skewers in the course and skip them.
en.plan_line: Book ahead, evening is course only, check year-end opening
en.baby_block: Adults only evening, maybe stairs, check first

en.hype: Digital art rooms you walk through water in, ruling the TikTok and Instagram feeds.
en.reality: Worth the money for a first visit, but at midday on weekdays the queues are long. If you've already been to teamLab elsewhere, it may feel like a photo tourist trap.
en.tip: Book the first slot and wear clothes that can get wet, because you have to roll up your trousers.
en.todo: Leave your shoes in a locker and go barefoot from room to room. You walk through knee-deep water, in rooms with mirrors and lights, and in a garden with orchids floating overhead.
en.special: Digital art you're inside of, with water, mirrors and lights that react to your movement, not an exhibition you look at from the side.
en.plan_line: Arrive before opening, midday on weekdays the queue is long
en.baby_block: No strollers inside, carry baby barefoot through water

en.hype: A gold-covered pavilion, on every Kyoto must-do list and in every Instagram feed.
en.reality: Reviews are mostly positive, but people complain about the crowds and the touristy feel, and some say it's a bit overrated.
en.tip: Look at the pavilion from the pond side and move on. School groups fill the entrance fast.
en.plan_line: Come at the 9:00 opening, before the tour buses

en.hype: High-quality, highly rated clear ramen.
en.reality: There's usually a queue.
en.tip: Get the ramen with porcini or with the yuzu egg.
en.baby_notes: Small place with a bar, not comfortable with a stroller.
en.serves: Clear, delicate ramen, a transparent broth with noodles. You can add porcini or a yuzu egg.
en.kosher_note: The broth sometimes includes fish and pork chashu, so ask.
en.plan_line: No bookings, closed Mondays, come before 11:00 to avoid the queue
en.baby_block: Tiny shop with a standing queue, no stroller

en.hype: A long-running gyoza place, steamed or fried, at ridiculously low prices.
en.reality: Loud and not very clean, and that's part of the charm.
en.tip: Order both the steamed and the fried.
en.baby_notes: Loud and crowded, not comfortable for a stroller or a baby.
en.serves: Gyoza are Japanese dumplings filled with meat and vegetables, steamed or fried. Here they're the main dish, and very cheap.
en.kosher_note: The usual filling is pork, so almost everything is out for anyone who avoids pork.
en.plan_line: Open daily, queue at lunch, come before 12:00

en.hype: A classic workers' izakaya.
en.tip: Order skewers and beer in the evening.
en.baby_notes: A crowded, smoky izakaya, not suitable for a stroller.
en.serves: Grilled meat skewers and small dishes, with no focus on fish.
en.kosher_note: Many of the skewers are pork or offal, so ask for chicken or beef.
en.plan_line: Yakiton under the tracks, arrive at 16:00 to get a spot
en.baby_block: Crowded and smoky under the tracks, hard with a stroller

en.hype: The torii gate path, in every Kyoto feed on TikTok and Instagram.
en.reality: Still worth seeing, but the main path is very crowded during the day. After a 15–20 minute climb past the first gates the crowd thins out, and the upper path is quieter and more wooded.
en.tip: Come around 5:30–7:00 in the morning, when most visitors are local, and keep climbing to the quieter gates.
en.todo: Entry to the grounds, in south Kyoto, is free. You climb the path of red torii gates along Mount Inari. The path branches, and you can walk it from half an hour to two hours uphill, with food stalls and fox statues on the way.
en.special: Thousands of red torii gates, packed like a tunnel, each donated by a business or a person. The shrine is dedicated to the god of rice and prosperity, and the foxes are his messengers.
en.plan_line: Open 24 hours, best to climb before 7:00
en.baby_block: Upper part is stairs only, stroller only at the bottom

en.hype: Yuba rolls instead of seaweed, with wagyu or sea bream, the dish people post from Nikko.
en.reality: Considered the top yuba restaurant in Nikko, and sets with yuba may need a booking.
en.tip: Get the lunch set with yuba and Tochigi beef maki, and come early because the options shrink in the evening.
en.serves: Yuba is the delicate soy skin that forms when soy milk is heated, and here it wraps rice and fillings instead of seaweed. There's Tochigi wagyu beef with a wasabi leaf, tai (Japanese sea bream), and a vegetarian version. At lunch you get a roll with soup, small dishes and pickles, and hot yuba zenzai for dessert.
en.todo: The place is small and sometimes has a queue, especially on weekends. Sets start at about ¥2,500, and cost more in the evening. It's a restaurant with tables, better for a baby than a bar.
en.special: Specializes in one thing, yuba maki, in a sushi-roll format.
en.kosher_note: Soy skin rolls with beef, tai (Japanese sea bream) or vegetarian, all fine.
en.plan_line: Closed Tuesdays, better to book for lunch

en.hype: The best depachika (department store food hall) in the Kansai area.
en.reality: Floors B1 and B2 are full of sweets, pastries and high-end ready food, and there's a floor of alcohol and tea too. Prices are high, but the quality and the packaging make it a good place for gifts.
en.tip: Come early, before the food floor fills up after work. From November 2026 you pay full price and claim a tax refund at the airport.
en.baby_notes: There's a nursing and baby room on floor 11 and stroller space on floor 1. The floors are wide, and it's less crowded in the morning.
en.todo: Go down to B1, buy sweets and pastries, eat something ready-made and sit. Then go up to check the homewares and fashion floors.
en.special: One of the biggest and best-organized food halls in Japan, with counters for tourists on B1 and the first floor.
en.plan_line: Mornings are quieter, keep passport and receipts for tax refund

en.hype: Top-level udon, everything made seriously, and the queue is tough.
en.reality: The queue is long, and at peak hours you wait a lot.
en.tip: Try as many dishes as you can, including the tempura made to order.
en.baby_notes: Small place with a long queue outside, not suitable for a stroller.
en.serves: Udon is thick wheat noodles, and here they come in a range of dishes, including fresh tempura made to order. Sometimes there's carbonara-style udon too.
en.kosher_note: Carbonara usually has bacon, so don't order it. Vegetable tempura is safer.
en.plan_line: Small place, better to come outside lunch hours
en.baby_block: Small place, queue outside, no stroller

en.hype: A high-level but very approachable sushi place, a good spot to start and get the full ritual without hassle.
en.reality: Only 8 seats, and the price is fairly high.
en.tip: Book ahead and tell the chef about food restrictions before your visit.
en.baby_notes: 8 counter seats, no room for a stroller, and the quiet isn't right for a baby.
en.serves: High-level omakase sushi. The chef serves piece after piece and usually explains in English.
en.kosher_note: Ask ahead for no shrimp, octopus, squid, shellfish, sea urchin or eel, and eat the other fish.
en.plan_line: Booking required, for lunch or dinner
en.baby_block: 8-seat counter, no stroller

en.hype: A cool place with posters and retro toys on the walls, and udon with tempura you shouldn't miss.
en.tip: Order udon with tempura and take a moment to look at the walls.
en.baby_notes: Small place packed with stuff on the walls, not much room for a stroller.
en.serves: Udon with tempura: thick wheat noodles in broth, with crisp fried vegetables or fish. A retro, colorful mood.
en.kosher_note: The udon broth is fish-based, which is fine for you. For the tempura choose vegetables, chicken or fish and skip the shrimp.
en.plan_line: Small place with a queue, come before noon

en.hype: A chicken restaurant with excellent yakitori, including raw egg yolk.
en.tip: Order yakitori and ask for the raw egg yolk.
en.baby_notes: Small izakaya-style place, not suitable for a stroller.
en.serves: Yakitori are chicken skewers grilled over charcoal. Here it's quality chicken with raw egg yolk used as a sauce.
en.kosher_note: Chicken on skewers, ask for salt instead of sauce and skip the organ meats.
en.plan_line: No verified hours found, check Google Maps first
en.baby_block: Small izakaya, no stroller

en.hype: A long-established tea shop with a very large teaware section.
en.tip: Get packaged green tea as a gift.
en.baby_notes: Small central shop, less suitable for a stroller.
en.todo: Browse the types of tea and pick some teaware.
en.special: An old shop that specializes in Japanese tea.
en.plan_line: On a Yanaka walk, check hours on Google Maps

en.hype: A tea house that claims to be among the oldest in Japan, in a merchant building from 1672.
en.reality: People praise the matcha parfait. The founding in 1160 is a traditional claim that hasn't been verified.
en.tip: Sit down for matcha and sweets, then buy tea to take home. It's across from Uji station.
en.serves: A tea house in Uji that specializes in matcha (powdered green tea). Order the matcha parfait, a dessert in a cup with ice cream, cream and bitter-sweet matcha. There's also a sweets and tea set, and matcha ice cream to go.
en.todo: A few minutes' walk from Keihan Uji station, and you can most likely just walk in. Exact price and hours aren't known, so check before you go. A good short stop on a day trip, even with a baby.
en.special: The 1672 building is a real historic site.
en.kosher_note: Tea house and matcha desserts, no pork and no seafood.
en.plan_line: By the bridge, come before noon to avoid waiting

en.hype: A view of the sand spit, almost no tourists.
en.reality: Far from Kyoto, about two hours each way, so it's almost a full day.
en.tip: Go up by cable car or lift to the viewpoint and look at the view from above, in the traditional pose.
en.baby_notes: You can reach the harbor area with a stroller and go up by lift, but it's a long trip for a baby.
en.todo: You reach the beach of a long sand spit with pine trees. You can walk or cycle along it, and go up to a viewpoint.
en.special: The sand spit is counted as one of the three most beautiful views in Japan, and the place is fairly quiet compared with Kyoto sights.
en.plan_line: 14–17 Dec closed or chairlift out of service, check website
en.baby_block: No strollers allowed, bring a carrier

en.hype: Grilled scallops (hotate), tamagoyaki and kaisendon in every TikTok seafood video.
en.reality: Still crowded and touristy, but the stalls are real and the food is fresh. The crowds are like before Covid, so it all depends on timing.
en.tip: Come early, 6:00–8:00, before the crowds, and eat small bites rather than a sit-down meal.
en.serves: You walk between the stalls and eat as you go: grilled scallops (hotate), tamagoyaki (sweet Japanese omelet on a stick) and kaisendon, a rice bowl with raw fish. Everything is fresh.
en.todo: Very crowded at midday. You pay for each item separately, usually cheap, and it's best to bring cash. Many dishes are raw fish, and if you don't eat those you can stick to tamagoyaki.
en.special: What's left of the old big fish market, with real stalls and fresh food. Come hungry and taste a little of everything.
en.kosher_note: There's tamagoyaki and rice bowls with tuna and salmon, but scallops are not for you. Check what's in each stall.
en.plan_line: Come before 10:00, most shops closed Sun and Wed
en.baby_block: Very crowded, hard with a stroller, carrier better

en.hype: Excellent tonkatsu with very careful frying.
en.tip: Order a tonkatsu set and come outside peak hours.
en.baby_notes: Small place, not set up for a stroller.
en.serves: Tonkatsu is a breaded pork cutlet, fried crisp, served with cabbage, rice and soup.
en.kosher_note: Every dish is pork-based, so not suitable.
en.plan_line: Small neighborhood restaurant, better to come before 12:00

en.hype: Osaka's kitchenware street, which even chefs from abroad come to.
en.reality: A covered arcade about 150 meters long with around 50 shops of knives, pots, tableware, takoyaki pans and plastic food models. The Sakai knives are the main thing, and not easy to find at home.
en.tip: Check in each shop whether there's a tax refund, and ask if they can engrave a name on the knife.
en.baby_notes: The street is short and covered, but the shops are narrow and packed, so leave the stroller outside and go in by turns.
en.todo: Walk along the street and go into the knife shops, like Sakai Ichimonji Mitsuhide. You can also buy graters, sushi tools and a takoyaki pan. All about five minutes' walk from Namba station.
en.special: You buy professional tools at trade-shop prices, and it's far more interesting than a mall.
en.plan_line: Most shops close around 18:00

en.hype: Fruit-focused cocktails, with a fruit-peel butterfly on the glass and a seasonal menu.
en.reality: Tabelog score 3.8 (2022 list). Good for a couples' date, less for business meetings.
en.tip: You can't book a seat, so come early. The counter is good for watching the bartenders at work.
en.baby_notes: A small cocktail bar with a late-night mood that gets loud after 22:00. Not suitable for a baby.
en.price: About ¥4,000–5,000 per person, including a cover charge of about ¥880
en.serves: A cocktail bar that's all about fresh fruit: cocktails from seasonal fruit and citrus, like yuzu (a tart, fragrant Japanese citrus), and a fruit-peel butterfly on the glass. No kitchen, you come to drink and talk.
en.todo: There are only about 23 seats. Open from 18:00 until 2:00 at night, and an evening place, not really for a baby.
en.special: The bar of Yasuhiko Mizusawa, a former Japan bartending champion.
en.kosher_note: Fruit cocktails with no kitchen, so no worry about pork or seafood.
en.plan_line: Closed Sundays, better to arrive early in the evening
en.baby_block: Cocktail bar for adults, not suitable for a baby

en.hype: The main branch of the chain, known for baked sesame tofu and a chef's counter.
en.reality: One Michelin star and a Tabelog score of 3.66.
en.tip: A counter of about 10 seats. The place handles bookings itself, so contact the restaurant directly.
en.baby_notes: Counter only with about 10 seats, no known baby facilities or stroller access. Not suitable for a baby.
en.serves: Lunch kaiseki (a traditional Japanese meal in several small dishes) at the counter. The star is goma-dofu, tofu made from ground sesame instead of soy, baked or lightly fried, with a rich sesame sauce or salt and honey. Alongside are small dishes of vegetables, fish and rice.
en.todo: Booking required, there are only 9–11 seats at the counter. You sit at lunch in two seatings, at 12:00 and 13:45, and usually pay ahead by card. The counter is quiet and tight, so think about how the baby will feel there.
en.special: A one-Michelin-star restaurant in Kyoto, and its tofu is almost a signature. People who went talk about very good value for a starred kaiseki.
en.kosher_note: Lots of vegetables and sesame goma-dofu. Ask when booking for no pork or seafood, and they usually adjust the course.
en.plan_line: Book well ahead, closed Wednesdays
en.baby_block: Kaiseki counter, no stroller

en.hype: A traditional tea and sweets house. The matcha isn't amazing, but the atmosphere is, and the amazake is highly recommended.
en.reality: A quiet area fairly far from the city center, and on weekends there may be a queue.
en.tip: Order the amazake (a cold dessert of sweet red beans and agar) and sit by the garden.
en.baby_notes: A traditional Japanese house where you take off your shoes and sit on the floor, not suitable for a stroller.
en.serves: A traditional tea house in an old Japanese house with a garden, serving matcha and Japanese desserts like amazake.
en.kosher_note: Tea and sweet bean desserts, no pork and no seafood.
en.plan_line: Closed Wed and the 1st and 3rd Thu of the month
en.baby_block: Take shoes off, sit on tatami, no stroller

en.hype: A free, high view over the city, one of the best free views in Tokyo.
en.reality: The deck is on floor 45, about 202 meters up, and the south side has a cafe and a shop. The south deck is open 9:30–22:00, the north one until 17:30.
en.tip: The elevator to the deck leaves from the lobby on floor 1. Check hours on the website first, and come in the evening for the view.
en.baby_notes: There's an elevator from the lobby. Stroller access isn't confirmed, check the official website.
en.todo: Enter the Tokyo Metropolitan Government Building in Shinjuku and take a dedicated elevator straight to floor 45, about a minute. Walk around the deck with big windows in every direction. There's no ticket queue, just a light security check.
en.special: A panoramic view of Tokyo for free, from a huge building by Kenzo Tange. On a clear winter day you can sometimes see Mount Fuji.
highlights: Mount Fuji on a clear day
en.plan_line: Free entry, check the deck is open after renovations

en.hype: The biggest and best-known baby store in Japan.
en.reality: Huge selection: diapers, formula, bottles, clothes, strollers and carriers, plus corners to try products. Nishimatsuya is sometimes cheaper for formula and diapers.
en.tip: Most branches are in malls, so pick one near your hotel. Ask the pediatrician about formula.
en.baby_notes: Wide aisles, strollers can go in, and there are usually nursing and changing rooms.
en.todo: Go in with the stroller, buy diapers and formula for the next few days and look at the Japanese baby clothes. Ask where the changing room is.
en.special: A much wider baby range than a drugstore, including Japanese clothing brands.
en.plan_line: Tax refund with your passport at the register

en.hype: Craft workshops in old machiya houses: hairpins, chopsticks, knives and indigo dyeing.
en.reality: Across from Sanjusangendo, 5 minutes from Shichijo Station. Prices vary a lot between operators.
en.tip: Cheapest to start with a single-item session. Before paying for half a day, compare prices between operators.
en.plan_line: Workshops must be booked ahead

en.hype: A vintage toy shop that feels like a museum, worth a special trip.
en.tip: Come with no plans and look at the old toys.
en.baby_notes: Small, fragile shop, no room for a stroller.
en.todo: Wander between the old toys, to look and to buy.
en.special: Japanese vintage toys.
en.plan_line: Hours unverified, check before you go
en.baby_block: No stroller space, narrow aisles

en.hype: Kobe steak and hot Kobe soup, the Kobe meal everyone photographs.
en.reality: Rated 3.41 on Tabelog. A shop of the Kobe beef promotion board, run wholesale, so quality is reliable but not top tier.
en.tip: If you want something other than steak, try the hot Kobe soup.
en.plan_line: Lunch set is much cheaper than dinner. Book a table

en.hype: Tamagoyaki on a stick, a classic snack in Tsukiji Outer Market.
en.reality: An old stall from the Taisho era, worth the money. The queue moves fast, but the outer market is packed by mid-morning.
en.tip: Arrive before 9:00, get the thick one (atsuyaki) and eat while walking.
en.serves: Tamagoyaki, a rolled, slightly sweet Japanese omelet, on a stick. Warm and soft, tastes of egg. There is also a thick version (atsuyaki), like a fat slice of omelet.
en.todo: Wait in a short queue, pay and eat as you walk. Bring cash.
en.special: A stall from the Taisho era, about a hundred years ago, with the classic market flavor.
en.kosher_note: Sweet omelet on a stick, no pork or shellfish.
en.plan_line: Closed Sundays and Wednesdays, come in the morning

en.hype: A seafood izakaya near Yoyogi Park, barely talked about on social media.
en.reality: Tabelog rating about 3.35. Seasonal seafood, and quieter than the famous places. Good, not amazing.
en.tip: Good for an izakaya evening centered on seafood.
en.plan_line: Book ahead (Tabelog or phone)

en.hype: Quality yakiniku that isn't crazy expensive, with a relaxed vibe.
en.tip: Choose a set of cuts.
en.baby_notes: Yakiniku with smoke at the table, not suitable for a baby.
en.serves: Yakiniku: you grill quality cuts of beef yourself on a grill at the table.
en.kosher_note: Mostly beef. Check there's no pork and avoid offal dishes.
en.plan_line: Book ahead, may be closed in late December
en.baby_block: Grill smoke at the table, not suitable for a baby

en.hype: Two covered pedestrian streets in central Kyoto, with hundreds of shops.
en.reality: Shinkyogoku is more cheap souvenirs and teen shops. Teramachi is more refined: books, galleries, knives and tea. Crowded with school trips.
en.tip: Prefer Teramachi over Shinkyogoku.
en.baby_notes: Covered and flat, easy for a stroller even in the rain, but very crowded at busy times.
en.todo: Walk along Teramachi and step into the specialty shops, like tea, knives and dolls. You can continue to Nishiki and Shinkyogoku and stop at just a few shops instead of all of them. Works in the rain too.
en.special: Everything is close: Ippodo, SOU·SOU and Nishiki are within walking distance, so you can do half a day of shopping without transport.
en.plan_line: Weekday mornings are best, Saturdays and afternoons are packed
en.baby_block: Weekends: hard with a stroller, narrow aisles

en.hype: One of the best okonomiyaki in Dotonbori, a quiet choice away from the neon.
en.reality: High Tabelog rating. Check the current score first.
en.tip: Order the classic okonomiyaki and let the staff make it.
en.serves: Okonomiyaki is a pan-fried pancake cooked on a griddle: batter, chopped cabbage and egg, with pork or seafood. Topped with sweet brown sauce, mayonnaise, dried fish flakes and seaweed. It comes hot, soft inside and crisp at the edges.
en.todo: Sit at the griddle and the staff cook in front of you. At busy times there's usually a short queue. Not clear if you need to book, so check.
en.special: On a side alley, away from the neon. Comes up again and again on lists of the best okonomiyaki in Dotonbori.
en.kosher_note: Regular okonomiyaki has pork or seafood, so ask for a version with beef or cheese.
en.plan_line: Arrive before 16:00, the queue closes around 20:30
en.baby_block: 2nd floor, lift unclear, hard with a stroller

en.hype: Kakinoha-zushi, sushi wrapped in a leaf, is Nara's signature dish.
en.reality: The chef's grilled fish and snack set gets praise. One visitor arrived at a dark, closed building even though the app showed it open.
en.tip: If there's no seat, you can buy a takeaway box of kakinoha-zushi.
en.serves: Kakinoha-zushi is pressed sushi wrapped in a persimmon leaf: a slice of fish, usually cured mackerel or salmon, on vinegared rice. The leaf adds a light aroma. A lunch set gives you several pieces with different fish, sometimes grilled fish too.
en.todo: A lunch set is about ¥2,000 per person. At some branches it's mostly takeaway.
en.special: Nara's most typical food, and Hiraso is one of the old shops for it. The taste is delicate and a little sour, and some people find the fish not fresh enough.
en.kosher_note: Leaf-wrapped sushi with salmon or mackerel, no pork or shellfish.
en.plan_line: Closed Mondays, check hours before you go

en.hype: A cafe shaped like a treehouse, with a flower shop underneath. The most Instagrammable there is.
en.reality: The food is ordinary and average, people come mainly for the look.
en.tip: Just order something light, coffee and dessert.
en.baby_notes: Seating on several floors with stairs, in a cramped space. Hard with a stroller.
en.serves: Coffee, desserts and simple food from a general menu.
en.kosher_note: There are light dishes and desserts without meat, but check what's inside.
en.plan_line: May have closed, check on Google Maps
en.baby_block: Stairs and cramped, hard with a stroller

en.hype: An old takoyaki stand with a Michelin Bib Gourmand, recommended by every tourist guide.
en.reality: Takeaway only, and locals queue for it. Tabelog rating about 3.5.
en.tip: About five minutes' walk from JR Tennoji. You eat standing nearby. The secret is in the batter.
en.serves: Takoyaki: warm, soft batter balls with a piece of octopus inside. The batter is made with chicken stock, kombu seaweed and bonito. You can add takoyaki sauce, mayonnaise and more.
en.todo: Mostly takeaway, no seating. The queue moves. Eat it hot, that's the taste.
en.special: The main branch in Abeno.
en.kosher_note: Every ball has octopus and there is no alternative on the menu.
en.plan_line: Opening hours are inconsistent, check before you go

en.hype: A small tempura counter in a basement, reservation only, with unusual ingredients.
en.reality: Only nine seats, online booking only.
en.tip: Book early through Tabelog or autoreserve. Up to 5 people per booking, so plan your group size.
en.baby_notes: Basement counter with nine seats and a long course, no stroller space. Adults only.
en.serves: A tempura course at a small counter: each piece is fried in front of you, one after another, and arrives hot and crisp straight from the oil. Besides shrimp and vegetables there are unusual things, like ginkgo nuts and hokke (a lightly smoked Japanese fish).
en.todo: You can only book online, through Tabelog. The meal is a fixed course of about two and a half hours. With a five-month-old that's long, so think about whether it suits you.
en.special: Rated 3.97 on Tabelog and picked for the 2025 Tempura 100 list, despite having only nine seats. Unexpected ingredients set it apart from classic tempura.
en.kosher_note: The course includes shrimp, so ask when booking for no shrimp or shellfish. The vegetables, ginkgo and smoked fish are fine.
en.plan_line: Online booking only, up to 5 people
en.baby_block: No stroller space, adults only

en.hype: The birthplace of the maneki-neko, the waving good-luck cat, with rows of cat figurines.
en.reality: Quiet compared with the main temples.
en.tip: Come midweek, when it's not crowded. From Shinjuku it's about 20 minutes by train.
en.todo: Take the Odakyu line to Setagaya and walk to the temple. Wander the green grounds, between the three-story pagoda and the main hall, and reach the corner with hundreds of white cat figurines. You can buy a figurine and leave one too.
en.special: Hundreds of white cats in rows, in a quiet, local place.
en.plan_line: Come in the morning, the cat shop closes 15:00 to 16:30

en.hype: The famous Tsukiji sushi stall, on almost every list of places to eat.
en.reality: Long queues, and sometimes no seats that day. The meal itself is slow. The fatty tuna and the precision get praise. Check which branch you're going to.
en.tip: Moved from Tsukiji to Toyosu Market in 2018. If the queue is too long, try Sushi Daiwa across the way. Check market days.
en.plan_line: Arrive by 05:30, 2–3 hour queue, cash only
en.baby_block: Tiny counter, no stroller, hours-long queue in the cold

en.hype: One of the best places in town for Sanuki udon.
en.reality: The place is small, and the lunch queue can be long.
en.tip: Order the cold udon with tempura.
en.baby_notes: Small, cramped place with a queue outside.
en.serves: Sanuki udon is thick wheat noodles with a bouncy bite, cold or hot. You can add vegetable tempura.
en.kosher_note: The udon is in bonito broth. In the tempura choose vegetables, chicken or fish and skip the shrimp.
en.plan_line: Queue before opening, closed Sundays and holidays
en.baby_block: Hard with a stroller, small place and queue outside

en.hype: A German-style holiday market, with lights in front of Keyakizaka.
en.reality: In 2025 it ran from 22 November to 25 December, 11:00 to 21:00, free entry. It usually closes after Christmas, and the 2026 dates aren't known yet.
en.tip: The Keyakizaka lights usually stay on until 25 December. Check the official site first.
en.baby_notes: Open area with flat surfaces, easy for a stroller. Can be crowded in the evenings.
en.todo: Drink mulled wine or hot chocolate, wander between the stalls and buy decorations and food. Then see the lights, and you can go up to the Roppongi Hills shops.
en.special: A European Christmas market feel in the middle of Tokyo, which you don't find elsewhere on these dates.
en.plan_line: Arrive 16:30 before dark, queues are long in the evening

en.hype: A matcha shop with a limited-edition shared parfait, looks great on Instagram.
en.reality: A good specialty tea shop with a seasonal parfait that photographs well. The parfait is time-limited, so the menu you saw online may no longer exist.
en.tip: Check the seasonal menu first. A good stop between Kiyomizu-dera and Sannenzaka.
en.serves: A Japanese tea shop on the way to Kiyomizu-dera, focused on matcha (whisked powdered green tea). Most famous there is a thick, strong matcha latte. There is also a donut and matcha ice cream, and sometimes a seasonal parfait.
en.todo: A short visit, usually you buy a drink or ice cream and leave. You can check what's on now on the shop's Instagram, @gokago_kyoto.
en.special: One minute's walk from the temple, and the focus is all on tea. The parfait changes with each collaboration.
en.kosher_note: Matcha tea, latte, donuts and ice cream, no pork or shellfish.
en.plan_line: Open until 18:00, go after Kiyomizu-dera

en.hype: A well-known, long-running yakitori place, famous for its asparagus rolls and a sauce kept going since 1977.
en.reality: Tabelog rating about 3.40. An old place with private rooms, reliable but not a new discovery.
en.tip: Order the asparagus rolls. The private rooms suit a group of four.
en.plan_line: Book ahead, especially on weekends
en.baby_block: Basement, probably stairs only, fold the stroller

en.hype: Two covered pedestrian streets between Kintetsu Nara Station and Naramachi.
en.reality: Higashimuki is closest to the station, with souvenirs and Nara linen. Mochiidono is about 250 meters long, with around a hundred shops and no chains.
en.tip: An easy route: Higashimuki, then Mochiidono, then Naramachi.
en.baby_notes: Covered and close to the station, easy to stop to feed the baby and get back to the train.
en.todo: Walk along Higashimuki and then Mochiidono, and step into shops with ceramics, calligraphy brushes, Ittobori dolls and deer antler goods. Continue to Naramachi if you have the energy, and stop for coffee on the way.
en.special: Small craftsmen's shops you only find in Nara, on the way from the park.
en.plan_line: Most shops close at 19:00, busy in the evening and on weekends
en.baby_block: Some shops hard with a stroller: stairs, gravel

en.hype: Contemporary art in an impressive underground building, and good for families with small children.
en.reality: Strollers are allowed throughout the exhibition, and crying babies are not a problem. Check the policy first.
en.tip: Check the family day schedule. There is a cafe and coin lockers.
en.baby_notes: Stroller access throughout the museum, changing facilities, and a nursing room and kids' room in the B1 lobby.
en.price: Varies by exhibition, check the website
en.todo: The building is almost entirely underground, and even the entrance is built like a metal sculpture. You go down between floors to exhibitions of Japanese and international contemporary art. Exhibitions change, so check what's on.
en.special: An underground building that looks like a sculpture, on Nakanoshima island in the river. Much quieter than Osaka's tourist hotspots.
en.plan_line: Closed Mondays and at year end, open until 20:00 on Fridays

en.hype: A huge train collection and baby corners, a good base for a rainy day.
en.reality: Aimed mainly at older children, and on busy days the stroller parking fills up.
en.tip: Stroller loans are limited, so it's better to bring your own. There are lifts between floors.
en.baby_notes: Stroller loans at the entrance (limited), 4 nursing rooms with hot water for formula, changing tables, a soft play area on floor 2 (no shoes) and lifts.
en.todo: You enter a giant hangar with real locomotives and trains from every era, and in some you can climb into the driver's cab. There are driving simulators and a huge miniature train diorama. On floor 2 there's a soft play corner for babies, and you can go up to the roof for a view of the tracks.
en.special: One of Japan's biggest railway museums, with a steam locomotive you can climb on and a short steam train ride in the yard.
en.plan_line: Arrive at the 10:00 opening, fills up fast on weekends and holidays

en.hype: A hidden wine bar in a Kagurazaka alley, run by a geisha who still works.
en.reality: A real local place, not a tourist bar.
en.tip: Open 20:00 to 02:00, closed Sundays.
en.serves: A small, colorful wine bar in a Kagurazaka alley. They serve wine, and there is no food.
en.todo: It's in an alley off Kagurazaka's main street and hard to find the first time, so open a map. You come to sit, drink a glass of wine and talk to the owner.
en.special: The owner is a geisha who works in Kagurazaka, sometimes in a kimono, and the place feels like a home.
en.kosher_note: A wine bar with no food.
en.plan_line: Book a spot, the room is small
en.baby_block: Small night bar, not suitable for a baby

en.hype: Inari-zushi and dishes with shiso, Kamakura food that shows up a lot on social media.
en.reality: Tabelog rating about 3.37. The shiso millefeuille and the ikura get praise.
en.tip: Order inari-zushi and the shiso dishes. If there's no seat, you can take it away.
en.plan_line: Closes when the food runs out, don't leave it for late in the day

en.hype: A fine Japanese restaurant that spent years at the top of the Tripadvisor ranking. It adapts every dish to the restrictions you ask for.
en.reality: Suited to a proper sit-down meal, not a spontaneous drop-in.
en.tip: Book as soon as you know the date.
en.baby_notes: A quiet restaurant for a sit-down meal, less comfortable with a stroller and a five-month-old.
en.serves: A traditional Japanese meal in small courses by season, adapted to the restrictions you give when booking.
en.kosher_note: When booking, say you don't eat pork or shellfish, and the restaurant accommodates. Not certified kosher.
en.plan_line: Book ahead, closed Mondays and closes at 20:00

en.hype: A sake brewery area in Fushimi, with tastings and sake ice cream.
en.reality: The exhibits and tastings get praise.
en.tip: Take the train from Kyoto Station. A tasting tour covering several breweries is better value.
en.plan_line: Closed Tuesdays, Fushimigura tour by phone booking only

en.hype: Japan's longest arcade, 2.6 km of shops.
en.reality: Mostly for locals: hundreds of shops, street food, second-hand clothes, kimono and knives. Not for impressive shopping but for the neighborhood feel, and liveliest at lunchtime.
en.tip: Very busy at the end of the year and early January because of New Year temple visits, so come before that.
en.baby_notes: Covered and flat, good for a stroller, with lots of places to stop.
en.todo: Start at Minami-morimachi station and walk north with no plan. Stop for a small bite, buy a souvenir in the small shops, and finally peek into Osaka Tenmangu shrine.
en.special: A real neighborhood shopping street, at local prices. About 40 minutes' walk end to end, and you can leave at any station.
en.plan_line: Shops are open about 10:00 to 20:00

en.hype: Giant tanks and whale sharks, a family outing even babies enjoy from a stroller.
en.reality: Strollers are allowed, but the escalators and the exhibit route are awkward with a stroller.
en.tip: Come early on weekdays and check the feeding schedule at the entrance. Use the stroller in the first part, then decide whether to leave it at the information desk.
en.baby_notes: There are changing and nursing rooms, and a small cafe halfway along the route.
en.price: Under 2 free, ages 3–6 about ¥700, 7–15 about ¥1,400, adults about ¥2,700. Check before you go.
en.todo: Take the lift to the top floor and walk down a long spiral around a giant tank. On the way you pass Pacific habitats: otters, penguins, seals, dolphins and tropical fish. At the end you can continue to Tempozan pier, with a Ferris wheel and shops.
en.special: The giant Pacific tank with the whale shark, where you can stand in front and watch it glide slowly.
highlights: Whale shark in the giant tank
en.plan_line: Buy the ticket online and arrive at opening, before the crowds

en.hype: A lively street market with hundreds of stalls and deals.
en.reality: Still a place where Japanese people actually shop, especially at year end for New Year food. Very crowded in December.
en.tip: Stalls are open about 10:00 to 20:00. Come midweek and not in the last days of the year, when most stalls are closed. Cash is useful.
en.baby_notes: Narrow and very crowded in December, a carrier is better than a stroller.
en.todo: Walk along the street between Ueno and Okachimachi stations, eat something from a stall and buy nuts, fish and some clothes. Toward year end there are big discounts.
en.special: An authentic way to see market Tokyo, and at year end locals buy holiday food.
en.plan_line: 30 December is the busiest, arrive before 11:00
en.baby_block: Hard with a stroller, very crowded before New Year

en.hype: An endless maze of snacks, cosmetics and gadgets, open 24 hours.
en.reality: Huge selection and fair prices, but crowded, loud and confusing. Some items are cheaper at a regular drugstore, but it's still good for buying lots of small gifts in one place.
en.tip: Go up the floors by what you're looking for, not in order.
en.baby_notes: Very narrow aisles, crowded stairs and lifts, not good with a stroller. Better without the baby, or one couple stays outside with him.
en.todo: Go in and climb floor by floor with no plan. Look for flavored KitKats, cosmetics, medicine and gifts for friends, and leave with a big bag.
en.special: The easiest place to find small, cheap gifts, even late at night. The big, well-known branch of the chain.
en.plan_line: From Nov 2026 tax refund at the airport only, keep receipts
en.baby_block: Narrow aisles, crowded lifts, hard with a stroller

en.hype: A three-story building with all the Kyoto crafts under one roof.
en.reality: Mixed opinions: some find the prices high and the selection thin, others are happy with the quality. Cheap souvenirs are better bought elsewhere, and the place is mainly worth it for the workshops.
en.tip: Before buying a big item, compare prices in other shops.
en.baby_notes: Several floors with a lift, but workshops of 40–70 minutes aren't suitable for a five-month-old.
en.todo: Do a quick loop of the floors to look and compare. If you have the patience, you can reserve a workshop, like fan painting or woodblock printing. Souvenirs that Teramachi also has are cheaper there.
en.special: Convenient for seeing everything in one place and getting an explanation, less for buying.
en.plan_line: Open daily, closed only 1–2 January, demos until 15:00

en.hype: MUJI's global flagship, with a range you won't find in other branches.
en.reality: The building opened in 2019 and includes a store, a hotel, a restaurant and an exhibition space.
en.tip: You can eat quickly at MUJI Diner in the basement.
en.baby_notes: Big store with lifts and fairly wide aisles, good for a stroller. There is baby clothing too.
en.todo: Go floor by floor: clothes, stationery, furniture and kitchen. You can also pop into the exhibition space on floor 6.
en.special: The flagship branch, with products not in every branch and a wider range.
en.plan_line: Usually open until the evening

en.hype: The observatory in Japan's tallest building, with a 360-degree view and a great night atmosphere.
en.reality: Very high rating and not crowded: 4.8/5 from about 9,900 reviews on Klook. Less busy than Umeda Sky.
en.tip: Go at sunset, and on weekdays there are fewer people.
en.todo: Take the lift from floor 16 to the top floors, about 300 meters above the city. There is a glass-enclosed floor with a 360° view of Osaka, and a floor with an open-air area outside, which is cold and windy in December. Stay until sunset and watch Osaka light up.
en.special: One of the tallest towers in Japan, with a spacious observation deck.
en.plan_line: At the entrance, check for a 整理券 (queue ticket)

en.hype: A hiking route along a forested ridge between two mountain villages, popular in autumn with hikers and photographers.
en.reality: The forest and views get praise. Common complaints: steep stairs and an uneven path.
en.tip: Start in Kurama and finish in Kibune for a meal by the river. Take the Eizan train from Demachiyanagi, not from Kyoto Station.
en.price: Eizan train fare, the trail is free
en.todo: Visit Kurama-dera temple on the mountain and from there follow a forest trail with tree roots and steps to the village of Kibune over the ridge. Go down to the river, visit Kibune shrine and eat by the stream. At the end you can soak in the onsen in Kurama.
en.special: A real mountain hike close to the city, through an ancient cedar forest and between two temples, with far fewer tourists than central Kyoto.
en.plan_line: Start by 9:30, Kurama-dera closes 16:30, the trail is icy
en.baby_block: Not suitable for strollers, mountain stairs. Carrier only

en.hype: On the list of the 30 recommended restaurants in Tokyo, in the wagyu category.
en.reality: The price is high, even for yakiniku.
en.tip: Choose a beef tasting set, so you don't agonize over the menu.
en.baby_notes: Grill on the table, heat, and it's unclear there's room for a stroller.
en.serves: Yakiniku: you grill Japanese wagyu cuts yourself on a small grill at the table, with rice and salad.
en.kosher_note: Order beef cuts only and no pork dishes. Not certified kosher, and the grill is shared across all kinds of meat.
en.plan_line: In demand, book ahead for 17:00
en.baby_block: Smoke and grill smell, not comfortable for a baby

en.hype: An obanzai buffet locals like, with fresh Kyoto vegetables.
en.reality: An everyday local place. Less Instagram, more real Kyoto home cooking.
en.tip: A good lunch for vegetable-heavy obanzai, and a good choice if you want home cooking beyond ramen and kaiseki.
en.serves: Obanzai is Kyoto home cooking. A buffet of small dishes made from seasonal vegetables, some simmered and some stir-fried. Take what you like, without committing to one plate.
en.todo: Fixed-price buffet, about ¥1,150 at lunch and ¥1,600 in the evening. Check price and hours. There are several branches, and one has a 60 minute limit when full. Easy with a baby, since you can get up and take things at your own pace.
en.special: A real meal of the locals, not for Instagram, with the emphasis on fresh Kyoto vegetables.
en.kosher_note: A buffet of vegetables and home-style dishes, you choose what you want. Check there's no pork in some of the cooked dishes.
en.plan_line: Better to book a table, the buffet stops at 14:30

en.hype: Dry ramen without broth, which you mix well with all the toppings.
en.reality: Usually a queue at mealtimes, and the place is small with counter seating.
en.tip: Order the dry noodles, mix a lot before the first bite, and at the end ask for a little broth for the leftovers.
en.baby_notes: Small place with a counter and high stools, no room for a stroller.
en.serves: Abura soba or mazesoba: thick noodles with no broth, with sauce, oil and toppings, and you mix everything in the bowl.
en.kosher_note: The regular dish includes pork and fish powder, so it's hard to find anything suitable here.
en.plan_line: Lunchtime queue, come before 11:30
en.baby_block: Counter with high stools, no stroller space

en.hype: A walk along a canal with cherry blossoms, like a movie set, and easy to do slowly with a baby.
en.reality: One parents' guide recommends not taking a stroller on the stone surface and preferring the paved road beside the canal, and one parent did push a stroller there.
en.tip: A light stroller or carrier on the stone path, with the paved road beside the canal as a backup. Go early in the morning or on weekdays, away from the crowds.
en.baby_notes: Mostly uneven stepping stones, narrow in parts, and lots of benches for feeding and rest. The paved road next to them suits a stroller.
en.todo: Walk along a narrow canal in northeast Kyoto, about two kilometers from Ginkaku-ji to the Nanzen-ji area. The path runs between trees and small houses, with cafes and shops on the sides. Walk slowly and stop at the benches.
en.special: There is no single attraction, it's a quiet walk beside a canal. The name comes from the philosopher who walked here to think.
en.plan_line: Start at Ginkaku-ji before 16:30 and head south

en.hype: A hidden onigiri stand for office workers, easy to miss. The rice is tasty and the fillings generous.
en.reality: More expensive than a convenience store but much tastier, and the place is small.
en.tip: Take a few onigiri and eat outside.
en.baby_notes: Small stand with no seating, not comfortable for a stroller.
en.serves: Onigiri, filled rice balls, at a small stand in an office district.
en.kosher_note: Choose salmon, umeboshi or seaweed, and skip mentaiko, shrimp and sea urchin.
en.plan_line: Come early, before the selection thins out

en.hype: Beef cutlet you cook yourself on a small hot plate at the table.
en.reality: Usually a queue at mealtimes, and the place is small and crowded.
en.tip: If the queue is long, ask about a nearby branch.
en.baby_notes: Small, crowded place with narrow tables, hard to get a stroller in.
en.serves: Gyukatsu is beef in a breadcrumb coating, fried briefly and served medium rare. You sear each slice on a hot plate to your liking, with rice, soup and cabbage.
en.kosher_note: All beef, with rice, cabbage and miso soup, no pork or shellfish.
en.plan_line: Arrive about 20 minutes before opening, no reservations
en.baby_block: Basement, hard with a stroller, queue at peak

en.hype: Rows of red torii gates and azalea paths, the picture of "Kyoto without the crowds".
en.reality: A hidden shrine with far fewer visitors than the famous shrines, with a history going back to 1705.
en.tip: In April there is an azalea festival, otherwise go on a weekday morning. The torii tunnel is the photo spot.
en.todo: Enter through a red torii gate into a courtyard with the old buildings, all in red and gold. Go down to a small path with densely packed red torii gates, and finish with a loop around the pond and garden. You can combine this with a walk in the Yanaka and Nezu neighborhoods.
en.special: Eighteenth-century buildings that survived almost as they were, and are counted as cultural treasures. In December there are no azaleas, but there is quiet and few tourists.
en.plan_line: Closes at 17:00 in winter, come before noon
en.baby_block: Stairs at gates, hard with a stroller. Carrier better

en.hype: A fishing village with boat houses on the water, pretty and quiet.
en.reality: Hard to reach by public transport, so best combined with Amanohashidate in one day.
en.tip: A short boat ride shows the boat houses from the water.
en.baby_notes: The village road is flat but narrow, and a stroller manages. There aren't many toilets.
en.todo: Stroll along the village with the boat houses right at the water. You can go up to a viewpoint or take a short boat trip.
