en.special: One of the few places in Japan where houses are built right on the water, without the tourist crowds of Kyoto.
en.plan_line: Buses are rare, check the timetable, boat depends on weather

en.hype: A quiet, uncrowded aquarium, easy with a baby in a stroller.
en.reality: A parent of a 7-month-old reported a quiet visit, less busy than other big aquariums in Tokyo. Suited to strollers and wheelchairs, but busier on weekends and midday.
en.tip: On busy days you can leave the stroller in the entrance area. Best on a weekday morning.
en.baby_notes: There is stroller parking at the entrance and a map of stroller-friendly routes. The nearest station is Kasai-Rinkai-Koen, a short walk.
en.price: Adult entry about ¥700, check the website
en.todo: A big aquarium on the bay, inside Kasai Rinkai Park, with a giant tank you can sit in front of, penguins and a glass house with a view of the water. Afterward walk in the park on the waterfront and ride the Ferris wheel. They plan a new aquarium to replace the old one, so check the website for what's open in December.
en.special: A giant tank of bluefin tuna swimming in circles nonstop, in a spacious place that suits a stroller.
en.plan_line: Closed Wednesdays

en.hype: A day-use private onsen with 19 private outdoor baths, among the biggest of its kind near Tokyo.
en.reality: It has no visitor rating, so it's hard to know how good it is.
en.tip: The main bath needs no reservation. Open about 10:00–20:00, and until 21:00 on weekends and holidays.
en.baby_notes: Not for a baby: you go in turns while the other couple watches the child. In the private rooms there is no crowd, and the tattoo rules are looser too.
en.price: Adults about ¥1,700 on weekdays and ¥2,000 on weekends. Private room about ¥9,400 for 2 hours (2023 figure, check).
en.todo: Arrive by free shuttle from Hakone-Yumoto station (about 3 minutes) or a 5 minute walk from Tonosawa station. From Shinjuku it's about 1.5 hours on the Romancecar. After the bath, stay to rest, eat something light and warm up.
en.special: An onsen by a river with about 19 private outdoor baths, no public naked bathing, and especially nice in December.
en.plan_line: Book a private bath ahead, no kids under 5 in the public bath
en.baby_block: Public bath not allowed under 5, private only

en.hype: Osaka's Akihabara, a center of electronics and anime.
en.reality: It started as an electronics district, but today it's mainly anime, games and hobby items. Only retro games and collectibles justify the visit.
en.tip: If you're not into retro games, you can skip it. Compare prices in a few shops before buying.
en.baby_notes: Nothing here for a baby, and a stroller doesn't fit in the small shops.
en.todo: Go into retro game shops like Super Potato, wander between the gachapon and manga shops, and if there's time stop at an arcade. New electronics are better bought at Bic Camera or Yodobashi Umeda.
en.special: If you like old consoles you'll find a big selection you can't get back home.
en.plan_line: Quieter on a weekday morning, go before 19:00
en.baby_block: No stroller space in the small, crowded shops

en.hype: A funny retro izakaya, with cheese-filled pancakes and shrimp cutlets that stick out of the batter. Popular with groups of young people.
en.reality: Tabelog 3.45 from 391 reviews. The food is fresh and fun, but the portions are small.
en.tip: Order the mini okonomiyaki sampler with nine pieces, the best value. You cook it yourselves at the table, which suits a group of four.
en.plan_line: Queue in the evening, book ahead. Mondays open at 17:00

en.hype: A maze of six blocks with tiny bars, the classic picture of Tokyo at night.
en.reality: Many of the bars are open mainly to regulars, but the atmosphere is worth it.
en.tip: Order one drink to start, and avoid the tourist bars if the cover charge is too high.
en.serves: Six alleys of tiny bars in Shinjuku, each with only a few people. You drink beer, Japanese whisky and sake, and some bars also have a small bite. Every bar has its own music and character.
en.todo: Most bars charge a cover, usually ¥500 to ¥1,000 and sometimes up to ¥4,000. Some accept only regulars, so look for a Foreigners Welcome sign or an English menu. It's not a suitable place with a baby, so either one of you goes alone, or you just walk the alleys.
en.special: The classic picture of Tokyo at night: a maze of small signs and three-stool bars.
en.kosher_note: Mostly bars for beer, whisky and sake. If there's a snack, ask that it has no pork.
en.plan_line: Bars open around 19:00, no eating or smoking in the street
en.baby_block: Narrow alleys, stairs, no access for strollers

en.hype: The white castle is a classic picture of Japan, and the most recommended day trip from Kansai.
en.reality: Worth the crowds. The main keep has scaffolding from July 2026 to July 2027, check the situation.
en.tip: While you wait you can walk around the outer grounds for free.
en.todo: Take the train from Kyoto or Osaka and wander between the gates, walls and courtyards, on a route deliberately winding to confuse attackers. Go in with your shoes in your hand, climb steep wooden stairs and look out of the windows. At the end you can stroll in the nearby Koko-en gardens.
en.special: One of the only original castles left in Japan, a World Heritage site, with the original wooden structure inside.
en.plan_line: Closed 29 and 30 December, last entry 16:00
en.baby_block: No lift, steep ladders, no stroller. Carrier is OK

en.hype: The original branch of Osaka's most famous kushikatsu chain, running since 1929 and in every picture of Shinsekai.
en.reality: 3.6 on Tabelog from over 1,000 reviews. The coating is crisp and not greasy and prices are low, but you can only dip once in the sauce, and the dish gets greasy toward the end.
en.tip: Always busy. The free cabbage helps balance the fat.
en.serves: Kushikatsu: small skewers of meat, vegetables and seafood in a breadcrumb coating, crisp and not greasy. You dip in a sweet brown sauce everyone shares. There is also doteyaki, a soft beef stew in miso sauce.
en.todo: Dip only once in the shared sauce. If you need more, take free cabbage, dip it and pour over the skewer. A skewer starts at about ¥143, and a set of 9 to 15 skewers costs ¥1,600 to ¥2,800.
en.special: The chain's first branch, from 1929, in the old Shinsekai neighborhood.
en.kosher_note: Beef, chicken and vegetable skewers are fine, but some skewers are pork and shellfish, so check each one before you order.
en.plan_line: Queue at dinnertime, no reservations
en.baby_block: Small, crowded place, no stroller space

en.hype: A moss garden with bamboo fences and a thatched roof, a quieter stop in Arashiyama, popular on Instagram.
en.reality: Quieter than other places in Arashiyama, but busy in autumn and the temple is small. Stay on the paths, don't step on the moss.
en.tip: Come early or on a weekday. The maple in autumn is the peak, and in winter there is sometimes light snow on the moss.
en.todo: Pay a small entrance fee and wander the paths in a garden all of thick green moss. Next to the garden is a thatched-roof hut, surrounded by maple trees. The place is small, so walk slowly, take photos and above all don't step on the moss.
en.special: A moss garden that looks like a green carpet, in a temple with a romantic story from Japanese literature, and fairly quiet after the crowds of Arashiyama.
en.plan_line: Last entry 16:30, best in the morning without the crowd

en.hype: Every Tokyo shopping list says it's the most beautiful stationery store in the world.
en.reality: The store is impressive, with a floor for each theme: pens, notebooks, paper, art. Japanese people shop there too, but each floor is small and packed, and it's not pleasant to walk around with suitcases.
en.tip: Floor 7 has a huge paper department with a paper advisor. Next door is another building, K. Itoya, for pens and art.
en.baby_notes: There are lifts, but the floors are crowded and the aisles narrow. Midweek in quiet hours it's possible with a stroller, on weekends better without.
en.todo: Start at the bottom floor and go up. Look at fountain pens, notebooks and special envelopes, and on the paper floor choose a few sheets by hand. Then buy small gifts for friends.
en.special: A range of stationery and paper that you almost can't find in Israel, including a whole floor of special paper.
en.plan_line: Easiest midweek in quiet hours, without suitcases
en.baby_block: Hard with a stroller at busy times, narrow aisles

en.hype: An 18-seat basement tempura counter that Tabelog keeps picking.
en.reality: On Tabelog's Tempura 100 list in 2022, 2023 and 2025, and 3.68 on one review site. Most TripAdvisor reviews are positive.
en.tip: Lunch is much cheaper than dinner, for the same tempura.
en.baby_notes: An 18-seat counter and an English-speaking chef. Adults only, no room for children.
en.serves: You sit at a counter, and the chef fries in front of you and puts each bite on your plate straight from the oil: shrimp, fish and seasonal vegetables, in a thin, crisp batter. There is also tendon (a rice bowl topped with tempura), and the chef explains each dish in English.
en.todo: Book ahead, online through Tabelog is possible. At lunch you pay about ¥3,000 to ¥4,000 per person.
en.special: An 18-seat counter in a Ginza basement that keeps coming back to the Tempura 100. Classic Ginza tempura without a scary level of luxury.
en.kosher_note: The vegetables, fish and the tendon with vegetables are fine. Ask for no shrimp or shellfish, and the chef speaks English.
en.plan_line: Closed Sundays and Mondays, lunch only on holidays
en.baby_block: Counter seats, adults only

en.hype: Tokyo's center of fashion and colorful crepes.
en.reality: Short, very crowded on weekends, and mostly souvenir shops and cheap fashion. Worth it mainly for a crepe and photos, and after a moment you head back to the station.
en.tip: If you go, do it midweek in the morning, then move on to Cat Street, which is calmer and has more interesting shops.
en.baby_notes: At busy times it's totally unsuitable for a stroller, because you move with the flow. Possible on a midweek morning.
en.todo: Enter from the station side, eat a crepe and look into fashion and souvenir shops. After ten minutes continue to the alleys and Cat Street, to independent shops.
en.special: The atmosphere and the closeness to the independent shops in the surrounding alleys, not the street itself.
en.plan_line: Best midweek before 11:00
en.baby_block: Not suitable for strollers at busy times, OK in the morning

en.hype: Tunnels of cherry blossoms over the moat and boats, the spring photo everyone wants.
en.reality: Magical at night, but very crowded at peak bloom.
en.tip: Go at night in late March or April, on a weekday, away from the crowds.
en.todo: Walk along the Imperial Palace moat on a tree-shaded path, with a few viewpoints over the water and the city. You can continue on foot to the Imperial Palace, right next to it.
en.special: Tokyo's most famous place for cherry blossoms over water, but in December not a reason to come specially.
en.plan_line: No blossoms and no boats in December

en.hype: A modern coffee stand with matcha drinks and desserts, and a stunning view of the Skytree.
en.reality: A small stand-only place, nowhere to sit.
en.tip: Get a matcha drink and enjoy the tower view.
en.baby_notes: Outdoor standing stand, you buy and drink next to the stroller with no problem.
en.serves: A small coffee stand with matcha drinks and desserts, and a view of the Skytree.
en.kosher_note: Matcha drinks and desserts, no pork or shellfish.
en.plan_line: Closes around 18:00, check hours on Google Maps

en.hype: A friendly izakaya specializing in tempura and oden, cheap and fun with a rough-and-ready vibe.
en.tip: Order tempura and oden with beer, and come in the evening.
en.baby_notes: A crowded, smoky izakaya with a rough atmosphere, not for a baby.
en.serves: An izakaya is a Japanese bar with small dishes. This one specializes in tempura and oden, cheap, simple dishes.
en.kosher_note: Oden usually has fish products. Choose vegetable tempura and don't order pork dishes.
en.plan_line: Standing bar with a 60 minute limit, near Ueno Station
en.baby_block: Standing bar only, not suitable for a baby

en.hype: Osaka's famous covered arcade, all the brands and drugstores in one place.
en.reality: A covered arcade of about 600 meters from Shinsaibashi station to Ebisubashi bridge, with lots of drugstores and cosmetics shops (Matsumoto Kiyoshi, Cosme Drug and more), plus Daimaru and Don Quijote. Very crowded, but practical because everything is covered and close.
en.tip: Not every shop gives tax refunds, so ask first. From November 2026 you pay the full price and claim the refund at the airport on departure, so keep your passport and receipts.
en.baby_notes: Everything is covered and flat, so a stroller gets through, but at busy times it's very crowded. Better in the morning.
en.todo: Walk along the arcade from Shinsaibashi toward Dotonbori and go into the drugstores for creams, face masks and supplements. You can go into Daimaru on the way and pop into Don Quijote for sweets and gifts.
en.special: A covered street that gathers all the easy shopping in central Osaka, especially useful on a rainy or cold day in December.
en.plan_line: Shops are open about 10:00 to 21:00

en.hype: Known mainly through Michelin and Tabelog, with no social media buzz.
en.reality: Tabelog score about 3.9.
en.tip: This is a formal kaiseki house, so dress and timing matter. Check the menu price before you book.
en.baby_notes: A formal kaiseki dinner with fixed courses. No information on baby facilities, strollers or a nursing room.
en.price: About ¥16,000 at lunch and ¥25,000 and up in the evening, check
en.serves: Kaiseki is a high-end Japanese meal, course after course, each small, beautiful and seasonal. Usually a clear soup, sashimi, something simmered and delicate, something from the grill, and rice and dessert at the end. The flavors are delicate, not heavy.
en.todo: You need to book ahead, and for a group of four book well in advance. The meal is fixed and you don't order separately. With a small baby, ask beforehand whether it's even possible.
en.special: Two Michelin stars (2024) and nine editions in a row of the Tabelog award. Top-level Kyoto kaiseki, in the heart of Gion.
en.kosher_note: Kaiseki with fixed sashimi and seafood dishes, so ask when booking for no pork or shellfish.
en.plan_line: Book a table ahead by phone or through the hotel

en.hype: A colorful retro cafe in Nakazakicho, with old, kitschy decor that does well on Instagram.
en.reality: People love the home-style lunch and the old-style pudding, but the scones and cookies disappoint.
en.tip: Go for the lunch set and the pudding. Nakazakicho has more than 100 independent cafes, so you can wander and choose a few.
en.serves: A colorful retro cafe, full of old objects and kitschy decorations. They serve a home-style lunch set and old-fashioned pudding, a classic Japanese caramel custard served in a glass.
en.todo: A small place with no information on reservations, so come at regular hours and see if there's room. Better for lunch. You can stop with a baby for an easy hour, if there's room for the stroller.
en.special: The decor is the story: old kitsch in every corner. A neighborhood cafe, not a chain.
en.kosher_note: Lunch set, pudding and coffee. Ask whether the set has pork and choose one without.
en.plan_line: Weekend lunch has a queue

en.hype: The quiet, less photographed lake of the Fuji Five Lakes, with a view of Mount Fuji.
en.reality: A calm option for anyone who wants to avoid the Kawaguchiko crowds.
en.tip: Works as an alternative to Kawaguchiko.
en.todo: Get there by public transport or car to the smallest, quietest of the five lakes. Walk along the shore and look for viewpoints of Fuji and its reflection in the water. You can have a picnic by the water.
en.special: The least touristy of the five lakes, Fuji without the Kawaguchiko crowds.
en.plan_line: Arrive for sunset and bring food, few options nearby
en.baby_block: Gravel path along the shore, hard with a stroller

en.hype: A tiny alley of cheap standing bars with kushikatsu, udon and takoyaki. Feels very local in the daytime.
en.reality: Cheap and fun, but in the evening the alley is crowded and touristy.
en.tip: Standing bars work fast, so order and eat fast.
en.serves: A small alley of standing bars in Shinsekai. Go for kushikatsu (skewers of meat and vegetables fried in breadcrumbs), udon (thick noodles in hot broth) and takoyaki (batter balls with octopus inside). Good food for beer.
en.todo: You eat standing and order from one of the stalls, no reservation. Come early, when there's more room. Less convenient with a stroller.
en.special: Cheap and local, and in the daytime it feels like old Osaka.
en.kosher_note: Kushikatsu is mostly pork and takoyaki is octopus. Vegetable skewers and udon are possible, but the broth sometimes has pork.
en.plan_line: Arrive before 17:00, before the evening rush
en.baby_block: Crowded alley, standing bars, hard with a stroller

en.hype: A vegan restaurant with Michelin recognition.
en.reality: The Tokyo branch is inside teamLab Planets.
en.tip: Check on the website how to combine the meal with the exhibition tickets, and book before.
en.baby_notes: Crowded exhibition area with water, less comfortable with a stroller and a baby.
en.serves: High-level vegan Japanese food, with no meat, fish or dairy.
en.kosher_note: Everything is vegan, so no pork or shellfish. No kosher certification.
en.plan_line: Combine with teamLab Planets and arrive before 12:00

en.hype: Gifts, packaging and stationery in bulk, with no tourists and all the signs in Japanese.
en.tip: Pick one or two floors according to what you're looking for.
en.baby_notes: Big building with a lift between floors, you can walk around with a stroller.
en.todo: Wander the floors of packaging, gifts and stationery, and pick only what interests you.
en.special: Eight floors, each on a different subject.
en.plan_line: Wholesale shop, closed Sundays, come on a weekday

en.hype: Top-level tempura, not cheap but exceptional quality. The chef is also a calligraphy artist who paints the menu.
en.reality: The most expensive of the places.
en.tip: Get the full menu.
en.baby_notes: A quiet, upscale restaurant with a bar, not suitable for a baby and a stroller.
en.serves: Top-level tempura: the chef fries course after course in front of you. Almost all vegetables and seafood.
en.kosher_note: The menu is built on seafood. There are vegetables, but this isn't the place.
en.plan_line: Must book ahead on TableCheck, closed Wednesdays
en.baby_block: Not suitable for a baby, 2 hour course at a bar

en.hype: Nihonbashi is an area of old shops and the long-running Mitsukoshi department store.
en.reality: The Coredo Muromachi complex has traditional shops: Kiya for knives, Ninben for bonito flakes and Hakuza for gold leaf, plus Mitsukoshi. Fewer tourists than in Ginza.
en.tip: Near the end of the year there are closures, so don't leave it for 31 December.
en.baby_notes: Modern, with lifts and wide aisles, easy for a stroller.
en.todo: Start at Mitsukoshi, move on to Coredo and step into the traditional shops. Buy bonito flakes or a knife, and you can eat something small at one of the restaurants.
en.special: You can buy from brands hundreds of years old here, without the crowds of the tourist areas.
en.plan_line: Check hours first, small shops are sometimes closed

en.hype: Considered one of Tokyo's five great nikomi places.
en.reality: The Tabelog score of 3.91 is from 2013 and not up to date.
en.tip: Order fast, eat and leave. One minute's walk from Keisei Tateishi station.
en.baby_notes: Tiny standing-style place, smoky and crowded, with a queue and an "eat and go" atmosphere. Not for a baby.
en.serves: An old neighborhood bar that specializes in pork offal: small motsuyaki skewers from the grill, and nikomi, an offal stew simmered slowly in soy sauce and mirin (sweet rice wine). Goes with beer or sake. Small, cheap dishes, and you keep ordering more.
en.todo: Arrive early and wait in the queue. They have their own ordering system and rules, so watch what people around you do. Motsuyaki and nikomi cost about ¥200 a plate.
en.special: A motsuyaki institution in shitamachi style, running for over seventy years, with a queue even before opening.
en.kosher_note: Everything is pork offal, no alternative.
en.plan_line: Cash only, no reservations, queue before opening. Closed Sunday
en.baby_block: Crowded and smoky, no stroller space, not recommended

en.hype: A slightly shabby building with tiny bars, like Golden Gai in Tokyo. Very Instagrammable.
en.reality: Small, quirky bars with a cover charge (about ¥300 at Dendo). Hours and venues change a lot, so the evening isn't guaranteed.
en.tip: Go in and try two or three bars, early in the evening is best. Check current hours because the venues rotate.
en.serves: An old building with tiny bars on every floor, each with room for only a few people. You order beer, sake or a cocktail, and some have small snacks. Every bar has a different atmosphere.
en.todo: Go in without a reservation and move between floors. The bars are small and smoky.
en.special: Reminds you of Golden Gai in Tokyo, but inside one building.
en.kosher_note: Bars with beer, sake and cocktails. If there are snacks, check there's no pork.
en.plan_line: Most bars open after 19:00, few seats in each bar
en.baby_block: Tiny, smoky bars, not suitable for a baby

en.hype: Back alleys of Korean yakiniku that no tourist map marks.
en.reality: The area is rated high for yakiniku and offal, but no single restaurant has a well-known score, so check each place separately.
en.tip: Order grilled horumon (offal). Pick a place with lots of locals and ask for the set menu.
en.serves: Korean yakiniku: you grill cuts of meat yourself on a charcoal grill at the table, mainly offal, the most local thing here, next to kimchi and sides. The smell of meat reaches you from the station.
en.todo: There isn't one recommended restaurant, so choose by the Google or Tabelog score. Good for dinner. With a baby, sit away from the grill because of the smoke, and check there's room for a stroller.
en.special: Tsuruhashi is a Korean neighborhood you feel on every corner, and not a regular tourist destination.
en.kosher_note: Order beef cuts and avoid the offal and pork belly, since many places also serve pork.
en.plan_line: Arrive at 17:30 before the queue, cash is useful
en.baby_block: Crowded alleys and charcoal smoke, hard with a stroller

en.hype: A view from above of the Amanohashidate sand spit and the Sea of Japan, and the ride down in the open chair lift is the most fun part.
en.reality: The view is impressive, but it's a small, busy park with simple rides, and the trip from Kyoto is about two hours each way.
en.tip: Go down in the open chair lift, not the monorail, the ride itself is part of the fun.
en.baby_notes: Carrier only, no strollers. There's no dedicated nursing room, so plan to nurse in a restaurant or the toilets.
en.price: About ¥1,000 per adult, round-trip ticket with chair lift and monorail
en.todo: Get to Amanohashidate station and go up to the park by chair lift or monorail, about 6 to 8 minutes. At the top you move between viewpoints and see the sand spit from several angles, including the famous "flying dragon" view. Go down in the open chair lift.
en.special: "Flying dragon" shows the sand spit from an angle that's hard to find elsewhere, with the sea and green mountains.
highlights: Small Ferris wheel in the park
en.plan_line: Chair lift closed 14 to 17 December, check the website
en.baby_block: Strollers not allowed, bring a carrier

en.hype: A sushi bar considered one of the best places for melt-in-the-mouth chutoro nigiri.
en.reality: The original branch is in Shiogama, far from Tokyo.
en.tip: Check which branch you're going to, because the menu may change.
en.baby_notes: An adults-only restaurant, and no information on whether it works with a baby.
en.serves: Sushi, sashimi and miso soup only. The popular nigiri is chutoro (tuna belly) and maguro (tuna).
en.kosher_note: The fish on the menu is fine, but there are also mollusks, shellfish and eel (anago), so avoid those.
en.plan_line: Tokyo branch is on floor 12 in Daimaru, book a table
en.baby_block: Adults only

en.hype: Tokyo's big flea market, 300 to 500 stalls, good deals on vintage and handmade ceramics.
en.reality: Almost every weekend in the Oi parking lot. Prices are flexible and haggling is expected, but it's all cash and there are not always card terminals.
en.tip: Arrive early to choose better, and bring cash.
en.baby_notes: Not suitable for a five-month-old: outdoors, crowded, cash only and canceled in rain. There is a nursing room with hot water.
en.todo: Wander the rows in the parking lot and the open areas, then go up to what's above the parking lot, where there are more stalls. In between you can stop for a snack from the food trucks.
en.special: One of Tokyo's cheapest and most varied flea markets: handmade porcelain, Pokémon cards, cameras and vintage jewelry.
en.plan_line: Weekends only and not in rain, check dates at trx.jp
en.baby_block: Not suitable for a baby, outdoors and cold in December

en.hype: A classic 1974 cafe with thick golden pancakes baked on an old copper pan.
en.reality: Small and local, and the pancakes are made to order, so sometimes you wait a long time.
en.tip: No reservations. Check hours before you go.
en.baby_notes: Small place with shared seating, and no information on strollers or a nursing room. A long wait is hard with a 5-month-old.
en.price: Two pancakes ¥700, coffee ¥450, about ¥1,000 to ¥1,999 per person
en.serves: Thick pancakes made to order, with butter and maple syrup, plus coffee and lunch dishes like Napolitan (pasta with tomato sauce and cheese).
dishes: Thick pancakes with butter and maple syrup
en.kosher_note: Pancakes and coffee are the safe choice. Avoid the Napolitan and sandwiches, which may include pork or bacon.
en.plan_line: Closed Wednesdays, opens at 8:00
en.baby_block: May allow smoking inside, check

en.hype: Neapolitan pizza, and the red tuna pizza is very famous.
en.reality: A short walk from Azabu-Juban station. Long queue on weekends. You can sit by the wood-fired oven.
en.tip: Come on weekdays, without the weekend queue.
en.baby_notes: Less comfortable with a baby because of the queue and the tight seating by the oven.
en.serves: Neapolitan pizza from a wood-fired oven. The red tuna pizza is the most recommended, and there are also margherita and marinara (with garlic).
en.kosher_note: Margherita or the tuna pizza, no pork.
en.plan_line: Closing day unclear (probably Wednesday), call first
en.baby_block: Small, busy place, hard with a stroller

en.hype: A giant aquarium around the Pacific Ocean tank, with huge tanks and whale sharks as the main draw.
en.reality: Crowded and loud at peak hours, but many say it's worth it.
en.tip: Midweek has fewer queues.
en.baby_notes: There are nursing rooms and baby beds in the toilets, but a stroller may be a problem, so bring a carrier.
en.price: Price not verified. Children up to age four enter free with a paying adult.
en.plan_line: Buy a ticket online, arrive at opening

en.hype: An elliptical Ferris wheel on the roof of Don Quijote in Dotonbori, with rotating cabins. The crazy idea works.
en.reality: The view of Namba, Abeno Harukas and Tsutenkaku is nice but not spectacular, and the ride is short.
en.tip: The pass that shortens the queue is sold in the store for ¥100.
en.baby_notes: The way up to floor 3 goes through a busy store, and there's no information on a stroller or lift, so it's not especially suitable for a baby.
en.todo: Buy a ticket and go through the first floor of the store, which is usually busy, and up to floor 3 for the wheel. The ride lasts about 15 minutes and gives a view over Namba.
en.special: The cabins rotate horizontally through 180 degrees, which makes it a weird, fun Ferris wheel.
highlights: View of Namba, Abeno Harukas and Tsutenkaku
en.plan_line: Cash only, check hours before you go
en.baby_block: May be stairs only to floor 3, lift unknown

en.hype: A gyoza chain considered one of the best in Japan, and the Kyoto branch has a separate vegetarian menu.
en.reality: Mixed opinions: someone waited an hour in a queue for average gyoza.
en.tip: Ask for a vegetarian menu in English and check whether the soup or sauces have pork or dashi.
en.baby_notes: Long queue and a small place, less comfortable with a baby.
en.serves: Vegetarian gyoza: vegetable (also vegan), dried tofu and yuba.
en.kosher_note: The vegetarian gyoza are fine. Avoid the pork gyoza and the chicken wings the Ginza branch is famous for.
en.plan_line: Long queue after 18:30, arrive before 18:00

en.hype: An izakaya specializing only in tuna, with an eight-course tasting menu.
en.reality: Open only in the evening, and you need to book about a month ahead.
en.tip: Make sure the sauces have no pork.
en.baby_notes: An adults-only evening, not suitable for a baby.
en.serves: An izakaya with a tuna-only menu. The main dish is yukhoe, tuna tartare with raw egg yolk.
en.kosher_note: The whole menu is tuna, a fish with fins and scales, but check the sauces have no pork.
en.plan_line: Book a month ahead by phone or online, cash only
en.baby_block: Adults only, narrow and loud

en.hype: A giant indoor Sega amusement park, with more than 20 rides and VR games, including a roller coaster synced to pop music.
en.reality: Most rides are arcade and game style, and suit mainly adults and older children. Mixed opinions, and considered pricey for the waiting times.
en.tip: Consider the evening passport. Re-entry on the same day is free.
en.baby_notes: With a baby who is only milk-fed you can enter with a stroller, but it's loud and crowded, so a short visit is better, or only the adults go in.
en.price: Entry about ¥1,500 to ¥1,700 per adult, unlimited passport about ¥5,800 to ¥6,000
en.todo: Enter the three floors of DECKS Tokyo Beach and choose between roller coasters and virtual reality games. Check in advance which rides are closed to strollers, and that long queues may be cut off early.
en.special: A mix of rides with music and rhythm games, like Gekion Live Coaster, which gives a score at the end of the ride. Good for fans of Sega, games and anime.
en.plan_line: Come early on weekdays, fewer queues
en.baby_block: Loud, crowded, many rides restrict under age 3

en.hype: Famous Cremia ice cream, made from fresh Hokkaido cream and milk.
en.reality: Not every branch sells Cremia, and the Dotonbori branch in Osaka has a good reputation.
en.tip: Call and check the branch sells Cremia first.
en.baby_notes: A short stop that works with a stroller and a baby, if there's a free spot.
en.serves: Cremia ice cream from fresh Hokkaido cream and milk, in a cone.
en.kosher_note: Dairy only, but check the kosher status with your own supervision.
en.plan_line: Sit by the window, with a view of the intersection

en.hype: A pancake cafe in Gion, famous for airy, melting souffle pancakes.
en.reality: The pancakes really are airy, but on weekends the queue is very long and the place is small, so it's better for a short breakfast than as a main destination.
en.tip: On weekends plan for a 40 minute to 2 hour queue.
en.baby_notes: Not especially suitable for a baby, since the place is small, queues are long and there's no information on a nursing room.
en.price: Pancake ¥1,200 to ¥1,500, about ¥1,000 to ¥1,999 per person
en.serves: Souffle pancakes, croissant waffles (croffles) and hamburgers. Sometimes there are limited-time seasonal pancakes, like matcha, hojicha and creme brulee. You order and pay at the register before you sit.
en.plan_line: Arrive before the 10:00 opening
en.baby_block: Small, long queues, hard with a stroller

en.hype: A Neapolitan pizzeria ranked first in Asia-Pacific on the 2026 50 Top Pizza list.
en.reality: Inside a shopping center, in a small space.
en.tip: Margherita with Jamba mozzarella instead of the Don Salvo.
en.baby_notes: Small space inside a shopping center, not much room for a baby.
en.serves: Neapolitan pizza. Don Salvo is a calzone (folded pizza) with ricotta and salami, and the margherita with Jamba mozzarella is the choice without pork.
en.kosher_note: Don Salvo has pork salami, don't order it.
en.plan_line: Closed Mondays, book ahead for the evening

en.hype: A small cream puff shop in Shinsaibashi that went viral, sometimes with long queues.
en.reality: The shell is crisp and the filling creamy, but some find the taste too sweet.
en.tip: Check opening hours before you head out, the information conflicts.
en.baby_notes: The shop is narrow and the queue outside is long, not comfortable with a stroller. Better for one of you to queue while the other waits with the baby elsewhere.
en.serves: Mini cream puffs with a caramelized, crisp shell, in boxes of 8, 20 or 30. There is also warabimochi (soft rice cake with kinako powder) and pudding.
en.plan_line: Come before opening, sold out by 14:00 and sometimes earlier
en.baby_block: Hard with a stroller: narrow shop, long queue outside

en.hype: Neapolitan pizza from the leading ones in Tokyo, on Tabelog's top lists.
en.reality: The dough is carefully fermented and the crust is charred and a little chewy.
en.tip: If possible, sit at the counter and watch the open kitchen.
en.baby_notes: Small, busy place, and no information on a nursing room, strollers or a private room. Better for an adults' dinner or a quiet lunch, and ask the staff ahead.
en.serves: Neapolitan pizza from a wood-fired oven, like the Japanese Umami with shiitake mushroom cream, mozzarella, pecorino, mackerel, katsuobushi (dried bonito flakes) and seaweed capers. There is also a veggie pizza with truffle paste and a soft egg.
en.plan_line: Book ahead, there's a queue at peak hours

en.hype: A pan-fried bread sandwich with egg salad, considered one of Tokyo's famous bites.
en.reality: A queue of 30 to 45 minutes or more, especially on weekends.
en.tip: Come before noon or after the peak, and wait in the park with benches across the street.
en.baby_notes: Not especially stroller-accessible, and the fillings are very sweet, but it's a quick stop.
en.serves: A pan-fried bread sandwich with a filling. The savory one is egg salad (tamago), and the sweet ones have cream or fruit.
en.kosher_note: The egg salad has no pork, but ask about the karubi meat version before you order.
en.plan_line: Check hours on Instagram

en.hype: Dubai chocolate souffle pancake with mochi and liquid chocolate, made in front of you and looks great on reels.
en.reality: The pancakes are rich and airy, but the place is very small, there are queues, and the egg taste is noticeable.
en.tip: There is room for only about eight guests, and on Instagram you can check whether the Dubai chocolate is available that day.
en.baby_notes: Small upstairs place, no information on strollers or a nursing room, so better to come without the baby.
en.serves: Soft Japanese-Western style souffle pancakes, with mochi and daifuku (stuffed rice cake) and a rich chocolate sauce. You can also order a set with a drink.
en.plan_line: Arrive at the 11:00 opening, sells out fast, no reservations
